proof_steps.full_text: If $P$ is empty, take the identity isotopy and stop. Otherwise extend $f$ constantly a little past the time endpoints; this is smooth by stationarity. The graph $S=\{(t,f_t(p)):p\in P,\ 0\le t\le1\}$ is compact, since a finite open-cover argument proves compactness of the product of two compact spaces. Its graph map is an injective immersion: the first coordinate retains $t$, and the source differential in $p$ is injective. It is a homeomorphism onto its image, since a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff space is closed. In local source and target coordinates, choose $k$ independent target coordinate rows for the $p$ derivative. Add the remaining $n-k$ target coordinate directions to the graph map. Its derivative is now an invertible $(n+1)\times(n+1)$ matrix, so [F2] gives a local product coordinate chart in which the graph is a coordinate $k+1$-dimensional plane, or its half-space at $\partial P$. The image of the complement of a smaller source neighborhood is compact and misses the graph point; shrink the target neighborhood to exclude it. Thus these graph charts describe all of $S$ near that point, with no other sheets. The same construction uses the constant time extensions at the two time edges. [F1, F2, given, construct]

Along $S$ the velocity $v(t,f_t(p))=\partial_t f_t(p)$ is a well-defined smooth target tangent vector. In a graph chart extend its coefficient functions across the source boundary using [F1], then constantly in the added normal coordinates. Target coordinate bases turn these coefficients into a smooth time-dependent vector field $v_i$ on an ambient neighborhood $O_i$ of that graph point, agreeing with $v$ wherever $S$ meets that neighborhood. Shrink $O_i$ inside $\mathbb R\times W$ and inside a time-target product chart with relatively compact target closure; a Euclidean coordinate ball with smaller radius gives the latter directly. Choose a smaller product-coordinate ball about the point with closure in $O_i$, and a nonnegative smooth Euclidean bump $\rho_i$ supported in $O_i$ and positive on that smaller ball. Such bumps are explicitly obtained from $e^{-1/(1-|x|^2)}$ inside a coordinate ball and zero outside, using nested balls if needed. Compactness selects finitely many of the smaller balls covering $S$, and only their finitely many associated fields and bumps are retained. This is a finite selection; no simultaneous choice over an infinite family is made. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

Put $\rho=\sum_i\rho_i$. It has a positive minimum $c$ on compact $S$. Choose a smooth scalar function $\eta$ zero for $u\le c/4$ and one for $u\ge c/2$. Define $$X(t,y)=\eta(\rho(t,y))\frac{\sum_i\rho_i(t,y)v_i(t,y)}{\rho(t,y)}$$ where $\rho>0$, and define it to be zero where $\rho=0$. Each numerator term is extended by zero off its bump support. This is smooth even across $\rho=0$, because it vanishes on a neighborhood of that set. On $S$ every nonzero summand equals $\rho_i v$, so $X=v$ there. The time-target support has compact closure in the finite union of the selected coordinate neighborhoods, and its target projection is a compact subset $K\subset W$. Multiply by one smooth time cutoff equal to one on the moving time interval and zero near $0,1$ outside that interval. This keeps $X=v$ along $S$, since $v=0$ on the stationary time neighborhoods, and makes the resulting $X$ stationary as a zero field near the endpoints. The finite bump sum and this explicit cutoff replace every use of a general partition of unity or global smooth Urysohn lemma. [step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

The compactly supported field $X$ has a global smooth evolution on this one time interval by a finite Euclidean argument. Cover $K$ by finitely many smaller coordinate boxes whose closures lie in larger coordinate boxes. For every box and every time in a fixed compact interval slightly larger than $[0,1]$, bound the field coefficients and their first state derivatives on its larger closed box by finite constants $M_i,L_i$, and let $r_i>0$ be the margin of the smaller box inside the larger one. The quantitative cylinder in [F3] gives a common positive time $\delta$ less than every $r_i/(1+M_i)$ and $1/(1+L_i)$; enlarge the compact boxes a little if their coordinate domains require open extensions. A trajectory starting in $K$ lies in one smaller box and exists for this common time in either direction. A trajectory outside $K$ is constant, since the field is zero there. At each later subdivision time, use the first smaller box containing the current state, in one fixed finite ordering; if the state is outside $K$, use the constant solution. Uniqueness makes all chart descriptions agree on overlap. A fixed integer $m>1/\delta$ permits continuation across $[0,1]$ in at most $m+1$ steps, in both time directions. Smooth dependence follows locally from [F3] and finite composition, independently of which box descriptions were chosen. Thus the maps $\Phi_{t,s}$ are jointly smooth and satisfy $\Phi_{u,t}\Phi_{t,s}=\Phi_{u,s}$ by uniqueness. They are diffeomorphisms with inverse $\Phi_{s,t}$. This is finite continuation with a predetermined number of steps; no dependent choice is used. [F3, step 3.1, construct]

Define $H_t=\Phi_{t,0}$. For fixed $p$, both $t\mapsto f_t(p)$ and $t\mapsto H_t(f_0(p))$ solve $\dot y=X(t,y)$ with the same initial value, because $X=v$ along the graph. Uniqueness in [F3] therefore gives $H_t f_0=f_t$. Every point outside $K$ is fixed. The zero field on endpoint neighborhoods makes the family stationary there; its initial map is the identity. If $P$ is empty, take $H_t=\operatorname{id}$ immediately. For zero-dimensional nonempty $P$, the graph charts have no $p$ coordinates and the same construction applies. All local extensions and bump parameters were extracted in one finite subcover; all integrations are the uniquely specified local Euclidean solutions composed finitely many times. This proves the choice-free assertion. [F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: First shrink the source parameter by $e_t(x)=e(r(t)x)$, with $r$ decreasing from $1$ to a fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and stationary near both time endpoints. For small enough $\varepsilon$ the last image lies in one chart about $e(0)$. Write its coordinate map near zero as $f$, with $f(0)=0$ and derivative $L$ invertible. Choose $m>0$ with $|Lv|\ge m|v|$, and $\varepsilon$ with $\|Df(y)-L\|<m/2$ for $|y|\le\varepsilon$. The maps $$f_u(x)=\varepsilon Lx+(1-u)(f(\varepsilon x)-\varepsilon Lx)$$ are embeddings: their derivatives are invertible and their differences satisfy $|f_u(x)-f_u(y)|\ge\varepsilon m|x-y|/2$. Their images lie in the chart after a further shrink. Write $L=QP$, with $Q$ orthogonal and $P$ positive definite. The path from $P$ to a small scalar matrix stays positive definite. It takes this parameterized ellipsoid to a coordinate round ball with parameter $x\mapsto\lambda Qx$. Stationarize the joins and apply [F1]. These are finitely specified paths. Small round balls can be moved along a finite chart chain: connectedness and local path-connectedness give a path between their centers, its compact image has a finite chart subdivision, and small translations and positive dilations in each chart give the required disk embedding paths. Apply [F1] to each path. [F1, F2, given, construct]

Pull the window to $S^{n-1}$ using the supplied parameter of $B$. Repeat step 1.1 in dimension $n-1$ for its full-dimensional disk embedding. Here the shrinking dimension is one for $n=2$, and the argument is unchanged. Move the small coordinate disk to a fixed pole and use a stereographic chart centered there. Its final disk parameter is $x\mapsto\lambda Qx$ in that chart. Increase $\lambda$ to the radius for a hemisphere; all disks in this path are embedded, and [F1] extends this isotopy of boundary disk embeddings to the whole sphere. Therefore the endpoint sphere isotopy sends the original window parameter exactly to stereographic $Qx$ on the hemisphere. Orthogonal $Q\in O(n-1)$ extends by the orthogonal symmetry $\operatorname{diag}(Q,1)$ of $S^{n-1}$; compose with its inverse if exact standard orientation of the disk parameter is required. This fixed symmetry extends linearly over $D^n$. The sphere isotopy itself extends over the ball by $$rx\longmapsto r\,h_{\alpha(r)t}(x),$$ with $\alpha=0$ near an inner radius and $\alpha=1$ near the outer boundary, and the identity on the inner ball. Its inverse has $h_{\alpha(r)t}^{-1}$ in the same formula, and it is smooth at the inner gluing sphere because it is exactly the identity nearby. Thus the window and its full parameter are standardized without an extension assertion for arbitrary sphere diffeomorphisms. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

Use that retained parameter to standardize the added ball's actual attaching map. A standard hemisphere window can be flattened in its normal collar to give a flat disk with a dome over it; interpolate the two graph functions while keeping positive normal derivative. Thin this dome by positive scaling of its normal coordinate. In the supplied receiving collar, use disk coordinates $x$ and inward coordinate $t\ge0$. After the specified corner rounding, the union with this thin cap has equation $t\ge\gamma(x)$, where $\gamma\le0$ is smooth and supported in a slightly extended disk chart. A full-dimensional disk parameter extends a little across its edge by [F2] and finitely many boundary charts: local smooth extensions agree on the disk, and a finite bump-weighted extension retains them there; its differential remains invertible, and compactness separates distant parameters, giving one smaller injective extension. These are only finite constructions. Choose a smooth one-variable cutoff $\rho(t)$ equal to one near the thin cap and zero beyond the receiving collar. Make the cap so thin that $\|\gamma\rho'\|_\infty<1$. Then $$ (x,t)\longmapsto(x,t-\gamma(x)\rho(t))$$ takes the rounded union diffeomorphically to $t\ge0$: its normal derivative is positive, its value on $t=\gamma(x)$ is zero, and it is the identity at the far end of every collar fiber. Off this coordinate neighborhood it is the identity. The inverse gives the removal statement with the same support. In dimension two $x$ is one-dimensional and the identical formula proves interval attachment. No general collar-existence or unmarked ball-identification theorem has been used; the required parameters and attaching collars were part of the input. [F2, step 2.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Parametrize the circle by a smooth regular embedding $\gamma:S^1\to\mathbb R^2$, and let $n$ be its smooth unit normal obtained by rotating and normalizing its tangent. The map $T(s,r)=\gamma(s)+rn(s)$ has invertible derivative at $r=0$. By [F1] and compactness it is a local diffeomorphism on a common strip $|r|<a$. It is injective after shrinking $a$: otherwise collisions for widths tending to zero would have a subsequence of their circle parameters converging; equality of the limiting images and injectivity of $\gamma$ give the same limiting parameter, contrary to a local inverse there. Thus $T$ is a smooth two-sided annular coordinate. [F1, given, construct]

We prove that a rounded polygonal region is a smooth disk. Take the finite triangulation in [F3]. The dual adjacency graph of its triangles, with an exterior root adjacent across every boundary edge, is connected. Indeed the triangles at any one vertex form a consecutive cyclic fan or a consecutive interval fan, so all their sectors are joined through shared edges, and connectedness of the triangulated region joins all fans. Choose a finite spanning tree of this dual graph rooted at the exterior. Process triangles in increasing distance from that root. Remove each triangle and its edge toward its parent: this edge is free, since its only other incident triangle has already been removed or is exterior. Removing a triangle with its free side leaves its two other sides and vertices, preserves connectedness, and preserves $V-E+F$. Plane Euler in [F3], with the exterior counted as one extra face, gives initial value $V-E+F=1$. At the end the remaining connected graph $K$ therefore has $V-E=1$, so it is a tree: a spanning tree already has $V-1$ edges, leaving no edge outside that spanning tree. [F2, F3, construct]

Inscribe a polygon with a sufficiently fine cyclic mesh in $\gamma$. Uniform continuity of $\gamma'$ gives positive scalar product of each chord direction with the tangent at every nearby normal projection, and the chord error tends uniformly to zero. Hence the normal projection of each chord is strictly increasing in its cyclic coordinate; the whole polygon has degree one under normal projection and is a normal graph. In particular it is embedded. Smooth its finitely many corners in disjoint small graph charts: convolution of the local graph function with a smooth compactly supported kernel on a smaller interval, joined by a smooth cutoff on a larger interval, leaves it unchanged outside that chart and can be made arbitrarily small in height and tangent direction. The smoothed curve $P'$ is still a normal graph $r=f(s)$, with $f$ smooth and arbitrarily small. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ supported in $(-a,a)$ and equal to one near zero. For $\|f\|_\infty\|\chi'\|_\infty<1$, the map $(s,r)\mapsto(s,r+\chi(r)f(s))$ is a diffeomorphism, because its normal derivative is positive, and equals the identity near the ends of the strip. It extends by the identity to a smooth plane diffeomorphism carrying $\gamma$ onto the rounded polygon $P'$. The same graph construction compares any two sufficiently small choices of corner rounding. By [F2], the polygon has bounded and unbounded regions; rounding preserves them by local graph homeomorphisms: in a graph chart, a continuous vertical displacement, cut off in the transverse direction with positive transverse derivative, carries the original piecewise affine graph to the rounded graph, and transporting them by the displayed plane diffeomorphism proves the corresponding separation and smooth boundary charts for $\gamma$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

Realize these finite collapses on smooth rounded neighborhoods. In affine coordinates on a triangle whose free side is to be removed, retain thin strips along its other two sides and a rounded disk at their common vertex. The missing sector can be chosen as a convex triangle with its corners rounded. Its attaching part runs along the inner sides of the two retained strips, joined around their common vertex, and is one boundary interval. Near the other two vertices use disjoint vertex disks and the corresponding short collar intervals; outside this triangle the neighborhood is unchanged. No other simplex meets its open interior. These choices give compatible rounded neighborhoods before and after the collapse whose difference is one smooth disk attached along one embedded boundary interval. To check that this added piece is a standard disk, a convex rounded triangle has a positive smooth radial boundary function $a(\theta)$ about any interior center. On the standard disk the radial map $r\mapsto r\exp(\eta(\log r)\log a(\theta))$ is smooth and linear near zero when $\eta=0$ there, agrees with $r\mapsto ra(\theta)$ near $r=1$ when $\eta=1$ there, and has positive radial derivative if $|\eta'|\,\|\log a\|_\infty<1$; choose its transition over a sufficiently long interval of $\log r$. Thus it is a disk parametrization. The corner models match the retained strip collars before [F4] is applied. Consequently each collapse preserves the smooth diffeomorphism type of the rounded neighborhood. A rounded neighborhood of the final tree is a disk: remove a leaf disk and its band successively, each a disk attached along one interval, until one vertex disk remains. Applying [F4] finitely often proves the assertion for the initial rounded polygon. Step 2.1 then proves it for the original smooth circle. [F4, step 2.1, step 1.2, construct]

Choose orientation-preserving disk parametrizations $p_i:\overline B(0,1)\to D_i$. The boundary map $p_1^{-1}bp_0$ has a smooth increasing angular lift $g:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, with $g(\theta+2\pi)=g(\theta)+2\pi$. Let $\rho(r)$ be smooth, zero near zero and one near one. The map $(r,\theta)\mapsto(r,\theta+\rho(r)(g(\theta)-\theta))$ is the identity near the center and has angular derivative $1+\rho(r)(g'(\theta)-1)>0$. It is consequently a smooth disk diffeomorphism extending the boundary map, and is a product in the radial collars. Conjugate by $p_0,p_1$ to obtain a preliminary extension. [step 3.1, construct]

We can replace either radial collar by its prescribed collar without changing the boundary. More generally, express two collars with the same boundary parametrization in the normal coordinates of step 1.1. Their relative coordinate map is $(s,r)\mapsto(S(s,r),R(s,r))$, where $S(s,0)=s$, $R(s,0)=0$, and $\partial_rR(s,0)>0$. Use the periodic lift of $S-s$ and interpolate to the identity by $(s+u(S-s),(1-u)r+uR)$ for $0\le u\le1$. At $r=0$ the Jacobian is triangular with positive diagonal entries $1,(1-u)+u\partial_rR(s,0)$. Smooth collar maps extend across $r=0$ in the normal chart, by their local smooth-extension convention and finitely many chart cutoffs. Compactness and the local-inverse and separation argument of step 1.1 give a common narrow two-sided closed annulus on which every interpolated map is an embedding. Reparametrize $u$ smoothly to be constant near its endpoints. Apply [F5] to this compact two-dimensional annulus and the ambient plane, with support in a thin boundary neighborhood. The prescribed isotopy fixes its middle circle, so its ambient extension fixes every boundary point and preserves the bounded side. Its final diffeomorphism identifies the two collar germs exactly. Perform this correction on both sides of the preliminary extension of step 4.1. The resulting extension agrees with $c_0(p,r)\mapsto c_1(b(p),r)$ on a common smaller collar. Its smooth inverse and orientation follow from the same properties of all the factors. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 4.1, construct]

For the interior prescription, first move $B(p_0)$ to $p_1$ by a diffeomorphism supported in $\operatorname{int}D_1$. A smooth path exists there by the disk parametrization of step 3.1. Cover it by finitely many interior coordinate balls and subdivide it so each successive pair lies in one smaller convex coordinate ball. For each pair, translation of a sufficiently small closed coordinate disk along their segment is an isotopy of full-dimensional disk embeddings whose track lies in that ball. Apply [F5], with a time parameter constant near its ends, and compose the resulting supported ambient diffeomorphisms. This moves the point as stated and leaves a neighborhood of the boundary fixed. Rename the resulting extension $B$. The germ $k=q\circ B^{-1}$ at $p_1$ fixes $p_1$ and preserves orientation. In centered coordinates its rescalings $k_t(x)=k(tx)/t$ for $t>0$ extend smoothly at $t=0$ to $Ax$, where $A=Dk(0)$, since $k(tx)/t=\int_0^1Dk(stx)x\,ds$. Each positive linear matrix $A$ is smoothly joined to the identity: write $A=RP$ with $P$ positive definite and $R$ a rotation, interpolate $P$ linearly to the identity and the rotation angle linearly to zero. Concatenate the resulting path from the identity to $A$ with $k_t$ from $A$ to $k$, and make the time parameter constant near the endpoints and all joins. On one common sufficiently small closed disk all slices are embeddings with track in an interior coordinate ball, by compactness and the inverse-function and separation argument of step 1.1. [F5] extends this disk isotopy to an ambient isotopy supported in that ball. Its terminal map $K$ agrees with $k$ near $p_1$, so $K\circ B=q$ near $p_0$. The boundary collars stay fixed. The attachments have actual convex disk parameters and explicit edge/vertex collars from step 3.1, exactly the marked inputs required by [F4]. All supported extensions use [F5], whose compact-track finite bump proof requires no choice. Thus all selections and compositions here are finite and no choice hypothesis has been added. [F1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: A smooth circle in the flat torus has a two-sided normal strip: rotate its unit tangent by $\pi/2$ in the oriented flat metric and use $\gamma(s)+r n(s)$ in local lifts. Its derivative is invertible at $r=0$; [F4], compactness and separation of distinct circle parameters give one injective strip. Subdivide its parameter into finitely many intervals lying in lift charts and replace their images by chords. Sufficiently fine chords have positive tangent projection and uniformly small normal error, so the resulting polygon is an embedded normal graph over the circle, exactly as for the inscribed polygon in [F2]'s proof. Normal graph interpolation gives a homotopy in the torus. The polygon is PL in a finite subdivision of the standard square triangulation (subdivide its finitely many crossings with square edges). It is essential and has the same homology class. Apply [F1]. Any two disjoint essential circles have proportional classes, since their algebraic intersection is zero; primitive nonzero classes with zero determinant agree up to sign. [F1, F2, F4, given, construct]

We give the finite bigon reduction with its smooth realization. Apply an integral unimodular linear torus map to put the common primitive class in direction $(1,0)$. Lift to the annular cover $\mathbb R^2/\langle(1,0)\rangle$ and then to the plane. Each reference lift is a proper horizontally periodic line in a bounded vertical strip. Its translates are disjoint. When two circles intersect, their signed crossing sum is zero; hence a segment of a lift leaves and returns to the same side of a reference lift. Among return regions choose one innermost with respect to the finitely many translates meeting this bounded excursion. Any further arc entering it has an innermost return through its reference boundary interval, giving a smaller return region. Reference lifts cannot enter without such a return either. Thus it is an empty bigon. Its projection is injective: translated boundaries cannot cross inside it, while strict nesting of it and a nonzero translate is impossible for bounded equal-area regions. The same argument for spanning arcs uses their strip lifts with the same translated endpoints; equal winding is precisely that matching-endpoint condition. A failure of a bigon in the presence of crossings would force all crossings of the two lifts to have the same sign, contrary to the zero crossing sum or the equal endpoint order. There are finitely many downstairs crossings after a small finite chart perturbation; that perturbation is a graph embedding isotopy, extended by [F3]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

Each empty bigon has smooth quadrant charts at its transverse corners, by [F4]. Truncate those corners, use [F2] with their prescribed boundary collars on the remaining planar Jordan disk, and restore the quadrants. This gives a lens chart with boundaries $y=0$ and $y=\phi(x)$, where $\phi>0$ between two simple zeros and negative just outside. For small $\delta>0$ and a cutoff $\psi$ equal to one between the zeros, the graphs $y=t\psi(x)(\phi(x)+\delta)$ move the lower arc smoothly over the upper arc, fixed near the endpoints of a slightly larger interval. Outside the two zeros the moving graph remains above $\phi$ wherever it could cross, since its difference is $\psi\delta-(1-\psi)\phi>0$. The empty bigon and a thin outer collar keep the track off all other curve portions. By [F3] this removes two crossings by a smooth ambient isotopy. Repeat finitely often. Disjoint arcs with matching endpoint lifts bound a disk strip; consecutive disjoint periodic circle lifts bound an annulus strip. To see both the topology and the smooth parameters, choose a simple arc between the two boundary curves in the strip, and cut along its period translates. Such an arc is obtained from a finite chain of coordinate disks by erasing repeated loops and smoothing its finitely many joins. The cut region is a bounded planar Jordan disk with paired cut-edge collars. Use [F2] to prescribe equal product parameters on the two cut edges and reglue; its quotient is a smooth annulus parameter. In the arc case there are no paired cut edges and [F2] directly gives the disk strip. Thus there is no merely topological annulus parameter being silently treated as smooth. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

For an empty family take the identity isotopy. Otherwise move disjoint curves across these smooth strips, and adjust their pointwise parameters by interpolating increasing interval maps or increasing periodic angular lifts. These are smooth embedding isotopies, so [F3] extends them. This proves the two-curve and two-arc assertions. For a finite disjoint torus family, first move one circle to an affine representative. Cut along it. The other circles are linearly ordered in the resulting annulus by their disjoint strip lifts. Choose the first remaining circle from one boundary. The strip up to it contains no other remaining circle. Use its smooth strip parameter to move it to a level in a small affine collar of that boundary, with support away from the boundary itself and from all other circles. That move has an explicit positive transverse interpolation in the strip, extended by [F3]. Regard this new affine circle as the boundary of the remaining annulus and repeat. This finite procedure retains every already affine circle and gives parallel affine levels for the whole family, using actual ambient isotopies at every step. All time changes can be stationary near their ends, and protected arc collars remain untouched by choosing bigons and strips outside them. Every selection, perturbation and reduction was finite. [F2, F3, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: If the family is empty, the identity isotopy proves the claim. Otherwise the explicit orientation double cover is $\widetilde Q=\mathbb R^2/\langle(2,0),(0,1)\rangle$, with free deck involution $J(x,y)=(x+1,-y)$. Two-sidedness of a circle means precisely that its normal line returns without a reversal; its tangent line is oriented by a chosen circle parameter, so the ambient orientation also returns without reversal. It therefore lifts to two disjoint circles interchanged by $J$, each projecting with degree one. Each lift is essential: a nullhomotopy upstairs would project to one downstairs. In the homology basis of periods $(2,0),(0,1)$, let a lift have class $(m,n)$. Its partner has class $(m,-n)$ up to orientation. Their disjointness gives $-2mn=0$ by [F1], and primitiveness gives either $(m,n)=(\pm1,0)$ or $(0,\pm1)$. Thus all lifts are horizontal or all are vertical; lifts of the two different types would intersect algebraically once and cannot occur in a disjoint family. [F1, given, algebra]

The torus bigon reductions in [F1] can be made equivariant. Choose a disjoint affine reference family of the same slope, paired by $J$. For horizontal type choose levels $c,-c$ away from $0,1/2$; for vertical type choose levels $x=c,c+1$. Take an empty bigon between an actual lift and a reference lift. Its $J$ image is another empty bigon. Their interiors, being components of the complement of the two lift systems, are either disjoint or equal. Equality is impossible: $J$ reverses the torus orientation, so on the boundary of an invariant disk it would be an orientation-reversing circle map, which has a fixed point. For that last fact a decreasing angular lift $g$ satisfies $g(\theta+2\pi)=g(\theta)-2\pi$, so $g(\theta)-\theta$ crosses a multiple of $2\pi$ by the intermediate value property. Also the two bigons cannot share a corner: their two corners lie on one actual lift, whereas $J$ sends that lift to its disjoint partner. A shared edge would likewise force a shared corner. Their closures are therefore disjoint. Perform [F1]'s smooth graph bigon move on one and the $J$-conjugate move on the other. Their supports can be chosen disjoint. These paired moves commute with $J$, remove four upstairs intersections, and descend to smooth ambient isotopies of $Q$. Finite repetition makes actual and reference systems disjoint. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

Now choose adjacent actual and reference circles of the same slope and their annulus strip containing no other circle. Its $J$ image is a different strip: invariance would require $J$ to preserve its actual boundary circle, since $J$ preserves the actual and reference systems separately, but actual lifts come in distinct pairs. The two open strips are disjoint. Their boundaries are also disjoint by the same partner argument. Use [F1]'s smooth strip parameter to move the actual circle to its affine reference, and make the identical $J$-conjugate move on the partner strip. These finite smooth isotopies descend. Repeating in the remaining strips, while fixing all circles already at reference levels, normalizes the finite family. If a chosen reference circle initially coincides with an actual circle, fix that pair and work in the remaining cut annuli. Paired compact-source extensions are provided by [F2]; smooth stationarizing time changes make all joins and endpoints jointly smooth. Vertical reference circles project to fibers. Horizontal paired reference circles project to two-sided curves transverse to every encountered fiber; invariant horizontal levels $0,1/2$, whose projections would be one-sided, were excluded. This proves the stated alternatives with no change to the circle-bundle coordinates or fiber structure. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

**Given:** The finite family of nontrivial groups in the Statement.

[F1] Every free-product element has a unique reduced syllable word; a nonempty reduced word is nonidentity ([[thm-normal-form-for-free-products]], Statement).

facts.full_text: Every free-product element has a unique reduced syllable word; a nonempty reduced word is nonidentity ([[thm-normal-form-for-free-products]], Statement).

proof_steps.full_text: Construct a graph $T$ with central vertices indexed by $g\in G$ and factor vertices indexed by the tagged left cosets $(i,gG_i)$. Join $g$ to $(i,gG_i)$ by an edge for each $i$. This graph is connected: multiplying a central vertex by one factor syllable gives a two-edge path through that factor coset, and [F1] supplies such a path from $1$ to every central vertex. It has no reduced closed edge path. Indeed such a path, started at a central vertex, alternates factor and central vertices. Consecutive central vertices differ by a nonidentity element of the intervening factor; otherwise the path immediately reverses an edge. Consecutive factor tags differ, since equal tags would again immediately reverse the edge at their common central vertex. A closed path would therefore give a nonempty reduced syllable word equal to $1$, contradicting [F1]. Thus $T$ is a tree. Left multiplication gives a $G$-action preserving both kinds of vertices and their tags. Every edge stabilizer is trivial, since fixing its central endpoint fixes the corresponding group element. [given, F1, construct]

A nontrivial element conjugate into a factor fixes exactly one vertex of $T$, its corresponding factor vertex. It fixes that vertex by construction; if it fixed another vertex, it would fix the unique path between them, hence an edge, which step 1.1 excludes. Every nonidentity reduced word $w$ can be conjugated to a one-syllable word or to a cyclically reduced word of length at least two: whenever the first and last syllables have the same factor tag, move the first to the end by conjugation and reduce the seam; the length decreases unless the word is already cyclically reduced or has length one. This is a finite process. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

For a cyclically reduced word $w$ of length at least two, concatenate, for all integer $n$, the two-edge syllable paths from $w^n$ to $w^{n+1}$. There is no reversal at a join because the last and first factor tags of $w$ differ. The resulting subgraph $L$ is an embedded bi-infinite path by the tree property. It contains the central vertex $1$, and $w$ translates it by a nonzero distance. It is the unique bi-infinite path on which $w$ acts as a nonzero translation. To verify uniqueness, project any vertex $x$ to $L$: the path from $x$ to any vertex of $L$ has a unique first point $p$ on $L$, independent of the chosen sufficiently distant vertex, since otherwise there would be a cycle. The unique path from $x$ to $wx$ is the concatenation from $x$ to $p$, along $L$ from $p$ to $wp$, and from $wp$ to $wx$. Hence $d(x,wx)=2d(x,L)+\ell$, where $\ell>0$ is the translation distance on $L$. On any other translation path the displacement is constant and its iterates give an embedded line. If that line were disjoint from $L$, its unique connecting path to $L$ would have to be carried to itself, forcing its endpoint on $L$ to be fixed. If it met $L$, their intersection would be invariant under a nonzero translation, hence contain the whole line: a connected proper interval, ray or finite segment cannot be invariant under that translation and its inverse. Thus the paths coincide. Conjugating gives the same existence and uniqueness for every element not conjugate into a factor. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

Suppose a nontrivial cyclic subgroup $C=\langle w\rangle$ is normal in $G$. If $w$ is conjugate into a factor, step 2.1 makes the common fixed set of $C$ a single factor vertex. Normality makes this vertex fixed by all $G$. This is impossible: a different factor contains a nonidentity element, whose reduced word is outside the stabilizing conjugate of that factor. More explicitly, after conjugating the vertex to $(i,G_i)$, any nonidentity element of $G_j$ with $j\ne i$ moves it by [F1]. Otherwise step 3.1 supplies the unique translation line $L$ of $w$. The group $C$ is infinite, since a nonzero translation has infinite order. For every $g\in G$, normality therefore gives $gwg^{-1}=w$ or $w^{-1}$. Their translation lines are the same, so uniqueness makes $gL=L$. Conjugate once so that the cyclically reduced description of step 3.1 applies; then $1\in L$. Invariance now places every central vertex $g$ in $L$. Every factor vertex belongs to the path between two central vertices, because its factor is nontrivial. Thus convexity of the line gives $T=L$. But a central vertex has degree $k$ and a factor vertex of tag $i$ has degree $|G_i|$. A line has degree two at every vertex, forcing $k=2$ and both factors to have order two, contrary to the hypothesis. Therefore $C$ cannot exist. All selected words, conjugations and paths use finite data; no selection over an indexed family is used. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

[F1] The Seifert local models are fibered solid tori, and their regular fibers are embedded circles ([[def-incompressibility-seifert-fibration-and-jsj-system]], Definition).

[F2] A finite free product of nontrivial groups, with at least two factors and other than the two-order-two case, has no nontrivial cyclic normal subgroup ([[lem-nonexceptional-finite-free-products-have-no-normal-cyclic-subgroup]], Statement).

A finite free product of nontrivial groups, with at least two factors and other than the two-order-two case, has no nontrivial cyclic normal subgroup ([[lem-nonexceptional-finite-free-products-have-no-normal-cyclic-subgroup]], Statement).

proof_steps.full_text: For any Seifert fibration the subgroup generated by a based regular fiber is normal in $\pi_1(M)$. Here is the transport argument including exceptional fibers. A loop can be moved off the finitely many exceptional cores: in each solid-torus chart perturb its finitely many subarcs away from the central one-dimensional core, keeping their endpoints fixed, and then concatenate. The regular part is a circle bundle. On a finite subdivision of the loop into bundle charts, transport a fiber around it; on chart overlaps a circle parameter changes by a circle homeomorphism of degree $+1$ or $-1$. The swept cylinders give the based homotopy relation $a h a^{-1}=h$ or $h^{-1}$. This also applies to loops crossing an exceptional-fiber neighborhood, since the chosen loop avoids its core and that punctured neighborhood is in the regular bundle. Compactness of the base and its isolated exceptional points makes their number finite: a finite cover by the local fiber charts contains at most one exceptional fiber in each chart. All perturbations and chart subdivisions used for an individual loop are finite. Thus the cyclic fiber subgroup is normal, without a need to orient all fibers coherently. [given, F1, construct]

Let $h'$ be a regular fiber of a second Seifert fibration, based on the same boundary torus. Step 1.1 makes $\langle h'\rangle$ a normal cyclic subgroup of $\pi_1(M)$. Its image in $Q=\pi_1(M)/\langle h\rangle$ is cyclic and normal, hence trivial by [F2]. Therefore $h'=h^m$ in $\pi_1(M)$ for some integer $m$. Since both loops lie in $T$ and $\pi_1(T)\to\pi_1(M)$ is injective, the same equality holds in $\pi_1(T)\cong\mathbb Z^2$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

Both boundary fibers are primitive nonzero classes in $\mathbb Z^2$. To check primitivity without a marking assumption, the boundary restriction of a Seifert fibration is an ordinary circle bundle $T\to S^1$. Cut its base circle at a point. The resulting annulus has the fiber as either end circle; a section over the cut interval joins any point to its image under the return map. Join that endpoint back to the initial point along the fiber and push the resulting loop slightly at the join. Its projection has degree one and its oriented intersection with a fiber is one. Thus a boundary fiber admits an integral dual class taking value one, which proves primitivity and nonvanishing. The equation of step 2.1 now forces $m=1$ or $m=-1$. Finally primitive equal unoriented homology classes on a torus are the same unoriented slope: lift two simple representatives to the planar cover, remove finitely many innermost bigons in a fundamental annulus, and the remaining disjoint essential curves bound an annulus. The annulus product moves one curve to the other; reversing its parameter accounts for the sign. Thus the two regular fibers have the asserted identical unoriented slope. Every choice in this argument is finite, and no triangulation of an arbitrary topological three-manifold is involved. [given, F1, step 2.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: The base is a compact surface with nonempty boundary. Its exceptional points are isolated, and a finite cover by local fiber charts shows that there are finitely many. Remove pairwise disjoint small open disks about them to form $B_0$, and remove their fibered solid-torus preimages from $M$ to form $M_0$. The restriction $M_0\to B_0$ is an ordinary circle bundle. The base charts away from exceptional points are ordinary disk or half-disk charts, and the quotient chart at an exceptional point is a disk with its marked center; these supply the base surface structure. Apply [F2] after choosing the disks, treating their boundary circles as boundary components. A locally trivial circle bundle is a Serre fibration here: a lifting problem on a finite cube is solved over finitely many subdivisions subordinate to trivializing charts, extending the already specified lift across successive parameter prisms using the chart product and retaining their common faces. Thus [F3] gives a surjection $\pi_1(M_0)\to\pi_1(B_0)$ whose kernel is the image of the fiber group, namely $\langle h\rangle$. In particular $\pi_1(M_0)/\langle h\rangle\cong\pi_1(B_0)$. Normality in the filled $M$ also follows directly from [F5]. [given, A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, construct]

Compute the base group while retaining the puncture generators. Join each of the $m$ new boundary circles of $B_0$ to one chosen original boundary component by disjoint embedded arcs. They can be constructed successively in a finite surface triangulation: choose an edge path between the desired boundary components, remove loops, perturb its interior off the boundary and existing arcs, and cut along it. Cutting an arc joining two distinct boundary components leaves the surface connected and reduces the number of boundary components by one; the inverse operation attaches a rectangular band along two intervals. The resulting cut surface $B'$ has nonempty boundary, is connected, and satisfies $\chi(B')=\chi(B_0)+m=\chi(B)$. A triangulated compact connected surface with boundary collapses to a finite graph: take a spanning tree in the triangle adjacency graph, rooted at an edge on the boundary; delete the root triangle across that free boundary edge, and then delete each successive triangle across its now exposed parent edge. Every triangle is deleted once and every deletion retains its other edges. The remaining connected one-complex is a graph spine. Collapsing a finite spanning tree in that graph gives a free fundamental group of rank $1-\chi(B')=r$, proving $r\ge0$. Restoring each cut band adds one free graph edge. Its loop may be chosen to run around precisely the corresponding puncture, with a path from the fixed basepoint along the joining arc. This follows also by covering the restored band and a small attaching collar by a rectangle: it attaches a one-cell between two points of the connected spine and no two-cell. Therefore, with these marked loops $c_j$ around the deleted disks, $\pi_1(B_0)=F_r*\langle c_1\rangle*\cdots*\langle c_m\rangle$. [F2, F4, step 1.1, construct]

Fill one removed fibered solid torus. The inclusion of its boundary torus onto its fundamental group is surjective, with kernel generated by the meridian: in its ordinary solid-torus coordinates the longitude maps to its core generator and the meridian bounds a disk. Hence [F4] eliminates the new core generator and adds exactly the normal meridian relation to $\pi_1(M_0)$. In the quotient by the regular fiber, this relation becomes $c_j^{q_j}=1$, up to inversion and conjugation. To verify the exponent, in the multiplicity-$q_j$ model the transverse disk covers the quotient base disk with degree $q_j$ off its center; its meridian therefore traverses the base puncture circle exactly $q_j$ times. Any change of its chosen boundary lift only multiplies by a fiber power, which is already killed. Repeating the finite fillings and then quotienting by $h$ gives $\pi_1(B_0)/\langle\!\langle c_1^{q_1},\ldots,c_m^{q_m}\rangle\!\rangle$. The free-product description of step 2.1 now gives exactly $F_r*C_{q_1}*\cdots*C_{q_m}$: a homomorphism out of either group is precisely a choice of images of the $r$ free generators and elements satisfying the respective relations $c_j^{q_j}=1$. Their identical universal properties give inverse isomorphisms. [F1, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra, construct]

Write $F_r$ as a free product of $r$ infinite cyclic groups. Under the numerical condition of the Statement there are at least two nontrivial factors, and the only two-order-two possibility is exactly the excluded case. Apply [F5] to any boundary torus with the specified injectivity. This proves fiber-slope uniqueness there for every other fibration, even when that fibration has a different base or exceptional multiplicities. The calculations also include $m=0$ and $r=0$ with the stated empty-product conventions. All topological constructions used compact smooth surfaces and already supplied Seifert charts; no topological three-manifold triangulation or full JSJ theorem was used. [A1, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: We record the circle-bundle coordinates used below. A smooth circle bundle over a disk or rectangle has a smooth trivialization. Construct horizontal lifts in each product chart and blend them by a finite smooth partition on the compact base. Such a partition is obtained by finitely many coordinate bump functions positive on a smaller covering family, divided by their positive sum; their linear combination of right inverses to the projection derivative is again a right inverse. Lift the straight contraction paths from a fixed interior basepoint to all other points. The resulting time-dependent vector fields have unique solutions by [F2]. They exist throughout the time interval: the total space over the compact disk is compact, the projected trajectory remains in the prescribed base path, and finitely many chart neighborhoods give a uniform local existence interval at every possible limiting point. Smooth parameter dependence and reverse transport give inverse smooth trivializations. At boundary corners use extensions of the bundle charts and restrict back to the rectangle; the prescribed projected paths stay inside it. For an annulus, cut the base along a spanning arc and trivialize over the resulting rectangle. Its gluing map has the form $(y,t)\mapsto(g_t(y),t)$ on the two cut faces, where $g_t$ is a family of circle diffeomorphisms. Orientability of the total space forces degree $+1$. Choose lifts $\widetilde g_t:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ continuously in the interval parameter $t$. The interpolation $(1-s)\widetilde g_t(y)+sy$ has positive $y$-derivative and period-one translation, so is an isotopy of these gluing maps to the identity. A smooth stationary reparametrization in $s$ may be used. Isotopic return maps have diffeomorphic mapping tori: if $f_s$ joins $f_0$ to $f_1$, the formula $(z,u)\mapsto(f_1^{-1}f_{1-u}(z),u)$ respects $(z,1)\sim(f_0(z),0)$ and the target $f_1$-identification. It is smooth across the seam when the isotopy is stationary near its endpoints. This proves the annulus assertion with explicit coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

The disk with no exceptional point is covered by the first trivialization in step 1.1, so its total space is $D^2\times S^1$. For a disk with one exceptional point, take a small fibered solid-torus neighborhood of that fiber. The remaining base is an annulus and the regular bundle over it is the product of step 1.1. Attaching this product to the neighborhood along its inner boundary merely adds a boundary collar: use the actual gluing map to parametrize the collar from its attached end, so no extension of an arbitrary torus map is required. Thus the total manifold is the given fibered solid torus with an elongated collar, hence a solid torus. This identification preserves the fiber direction on its boundary. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

For a Möbius base with no exceptional point, cut along a spanning arc. The rectangle trivialization glues by $(y,t)\mapsto(g_t(y),-t)$. The base normal coordinate is reversed, so orientability forces every $g_t$ to have degree $-1$. Continuous lifts have negative $y$-derivative; interpolating them to $-y$ retains negative derivative and the required degree. The same mapping-torus coordinate change as in step 1.1 identifies this total space with $W$. Forgetting $t$ exhibits $W$ as an interval bundle over $K=\mathbb R^2/\langle(x,y)\mapsto(x+1,-y),(x,y)\mapsto(x,y+1)\rangle$. It is twisted because transport around the first generator reverses $t$, and its total space is orientable because that generator reverses both $y$ and $t$. The $y$-circles have base $(\mathbb R\times[-1,1])/((x,t)\sim(x+1,-t))$, a Möbius band. These statements also directly construct its first Seifert fibration. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

The flow $(x,y,t)\mapsto(x+s,y,t)$ on $W$ has period two at every generic point. The points $(y,t)=(0,0),(1/2,0)$ have period one, and these are the only shorter orbits. Around either, the return map after time one is the linear half-turn $(v,t)\mapsto(-v,-t)$ on a transverse disk. They therefore give exactly two exceptional fibers of multiplicity two. Its orbit space is the annulus $S^1_y\times[-1,1]$ divided by $(y,t)\mapsto(-y,-t)$. A fundamental rectangle is $0\le y\le1/2$, $-1\le t\le1$, with each vertical side folded by $t\sim-t$. Split it at $t=0$. The two half-rectangles are disks glued along the three-edge boundary interval consisting of the left side, the $t=0$ side and the right side. By [F4] their quotient is a parametrized disk. The fold points $(0,0)$ and $(1/2,0)$ are its two marked interior points. Thus the second asserted Seifert structure on $W$ is explicit. [F1, F4, step 2.2, construct]

Now let $B$ be a disk with two multiplicity-two points. Cut it along an arc separating those points. Its inverse image is a vertical annulus $A$ splitting $M$ into two pieces of the one-exception disk type of step 2.1. Each is a fibered solid torus, and $A$ is a band around a regular-fiber slope on its boundary. In meridian-longitude coordinates that primitive fiber has class $p\mu+2\lambda$ with $p$ odd. The meridian twist $(z,w)\mapsto(w^kz,w)$ changes $p$ to $p+2k$; take $k=(1-p)/2$ to normalize it to $\mu+2\lambda$. This changes no prescribed outer marking because none is required. The band coordinates from the fibered boundary collar identify $A$ with a standard annular band about this normalized slope. The two solid tori and their marked annuli are therefore fixed standard pairs. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

It remains to check that their possible gluing maps give one underlying orientable manifold. A fiber-preserving map of their annuli has the form $(\theta,u)\mapsto(F_u(\theta),\sigma(u))$, with circle degree $\varepsilon=\pm1$ and interval orientation $\eta=\pm1$. Interpolate $\sigma$ to the corresponding affine interval map, and choose continuous lifts of $F_u$; their interpolation to $\varepsilon\theta$ retains nonzero derivative of the required sign. Thus the annulus map is isotopic, allowing its boundary circles to move, to $(\theta,u)\mapsto(\varepsilon\theta,\eta u)$. Orientability of the glued manifold requires $\varepsilon\eta=-1$. The two remaining maps differ by $(\theta,u)\mapsto(-\theta,-u)$. This latter map extends over the standard solid torus by $(z,w)\mapsto(\overline z,\overline w)$: choose its standard slope band invariant under simultaneous angle reversal, which reverses both the fiber and transverse band parameters. The preceding annulus isotopies also extend over that solid torus by [F3], using [A1]. Hence all allowable gluings are diffeomorphic. Step 3.1 constructs one of them in $W$, so every disk-two-order-two piece is $W$. The disk and annulus models were proved in steps 1.1–2.1, and the Möbius model in step 2.2. Finally a nontrivial interval bundle over an orientable torus reverses its interval direction around some loop and therefore reverses the total orientation; $K\times I$ is nonorientable because $K$ is. Neither is an additional orientable case. All model identifications were explicit finite constructions in smooth Seifert pieces. [A1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, step 3.2, construct] ∎

Removing exceptional-fiber neighborhoods gives a circle bundle over a surface with boundary; the base has a finite graph spine with a free basis containing the individual puncture loops. Filling the $j$th neighborhood imposes its meridian relation, whose projection goes $q_j$ times around that puncture ([[lem-seifert-fiber-quotient-is-finite-orbifold-free-product]], Proof 1.1–3.1).

The exact homotopy sequence of a fibration identifies the kernel on fundamental groups with the image of the fiber and injects the fiber group when the base has zero $\pi_2$ ([[thm-long-exact-sequence-of-homotopy-groups-of-a-fibration]], Statement).
Van Kampen computes the solid-torus fillings as group pushouts ([[thm-seifert-van-kampen]], Statement).

proof_steps.full_text: Use [F2] to write $M_0\to B_0$ for the regular circle bundle. Its base retracts to a finite graph, so $\pi_2(B_0)=0$: a map of a sphere to a graph lifts to the graph's universal tree and contracts there. The tree is the explicit reduced-edge-path tree, and the compact image of a lifted sphere lies in finitely many edge stars of this locally finite tree and therefore contracts in a finite subtree. By [F3] there is an exact sequence $1\to\langle h\rangle\cong\mathbb Z\to\pi_1(M_0)\to\pi_1(B_0)\to1$. Fix the free base generators $c_1,\ldots,c_m,u_1,\ldots,u_r$ given in [F2], the $c_j$ being the small puncture loops. Lift each generator to a loop in $M_0$; path lifting and an arc in its terminal fiber give such a lift, and only finitely many are selected. Freeness extends these lifts to a section of the group surjection. Thus $\pi_1(M_0)$ is the semidirect product of the infinite cyclic fiber group and this free group. [A1, F2, F3, construct]

A lifted generator conjugates $h$ to $h$ or $h^{-1}$ according to the fiber-orientation transport along it. The puncture loops $c_j$ preserve orientation, since their neighborhoods in the base are annuli and the total space is orientable. Put $\varepsilon_i=\pm1$ for the signs of the remaining $u_i$. Consequently the bundle group has presentation with generators $h,c_j,u_i$ and only relations $c_j h c_j^{-1}=h$ and $u_i h u_i^{-1}=h^{\varepsilon_i}$. This is exact, rather than just a list of necessary relations: the indicated semidirect product has unique form $h^n w$, where $w$ is a reduced word in the chosen base generators; its projection determines $w$ and the injected fiber determines $n$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

In the boundary torus about the $j$th missing exceptional fiber, $c_j$ and $h$ give a basis: its projection onto the puncture circle takes $c_j$ once around that circle and kills $h$. After conjugating along the chosen basepath if necessary, its meridian therefore has word $c_j^{q_j}h^{p_j}$, with $p_j$ an integer relatively prime to $q_j$. The exponent $q_j$ is [F2]'s local multiplicity calculation; primitivity follows because a meridian is primitive in the torus group. The inclusion of the filled solid torus's boundary onto its core group is surjective and kills exactly that meridian. By [F4] the presentation of step 2.1, with the additional relations $c_j^{q_j}h^{p_j}=1$, is a presentation of $\pi_1(M)$. No relation for an original boundary circle is added, because the free base generators were chosen after retaining an original boundary component. [F1, F2, F4, step 2.1, algebra]

Define an action of this presented group on the real line. Let $h$ act by $x\mapsto x+1$, let $c_j$ act by $x\mapsto x-p_j/q_j$, and let $u_i$ act by $x\mapsto\varepsilon_i x$. Translations commute, reflections invert the unit translation, and $q_j(-p_j/q_j)+p_j=0$, so every relation of step 3.1 is satisfied. The resulting homomorphism sends every nonzero power $h^n$ to the nonidentity translation $x\mapsto x+n$. Hence $h$ has infinite order in $\pi_1(M)$. Any other based regular fiber is conjugate to $h$ or $h^{-1}$ by transport in the connected regular base, so has the same order. Over a proper base arc the bundle is a product $S^1\times I$; its annular core represents this infinite-order fiber. The annulus is orientable, and in orientable $M$ its normal line is trivial, so it is two-sided. Its fundamental group therefore injects. An embedded compressing disk would make a nonzero power of its core trivial in $\pi_1(M)$, contradicting that injection. This uses no general Loop theorem or irreducibility of $M$. [F1, step 3.1, construct, algebra] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Let $S$ be a smooth embedded sphere in the interior of $M$. By [F2] make it transverse to $\mathcal A$; intersections are finitely many disjoint circles. Among all such transverse positions obtained by ambient isotopies supported in the interior choose one with the least number of circles. The set of possible counts is a nonempty subset of the natural numbers, so it has a least element; only one representative is selected. If the count is zero, $S$ lies in the interior of a cut piece and bounds a ball there by the Given irreducibility. Suppose instead that a circle $C$ is innermost on $S$, bounding $D\subset S$ with interior disjoint from all annuli. Its class is trivial in $\pi_1(M)$ and hence in the annulus $A$ containing it, by injectivity. By [F5] applied to the oriented open annulus, $C$ bounds a disk region $D'$ in its interior, unique because that component is not a sphere. Its inherited disk-region charts are smooth, since $C$ and $A$ are smooth. Lift this simply connected compact disk region to the standard strip cover of the annulus. The lift projects diffeomorphically onto it, and is the bounded region of its smooth planar boundary circle. Thus [F6] supplies an actual smooth disk parameter, with the boundary collar retained when needed. Thus $D\cup D'$ is an embedded sphere with a corner along $C$. [A1, F1, F2, F5, F6, given, construct]

The interior of $D$ lies on one cut side of $A$. Push $D'$ slightly into that side and round the rim along $C$. This produces a sphere in the interior of the same cut piece, hence a ball there. Restore the thin product collar between the pushed disk and $D'$: in the two-dimensional normal section at $C$ the two meeting half-disks form a quadrant, and its rounding has the same ball-window chart. Thus [F3] adds precisely that collar window and gives a ball $B$, allowing the displayed boundary corner, with boundary $D\cup D'$ and $B\cap\bigcup\mathcal A=D'$. This assertion concerns that particular side, not an assumption that an arbitrary sphere in $M$ already bounds a ball. It follows from the cut-piece ball and the restored window; all other cut faces remain outside it. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

We spell out the disk push across this ball. Standardize $(B,D')$ by [F3]; its complementary boundary disk is $D$. The two hemispheres of a standard ball admit a common-boundary disk sweep through its interior. For example, in polar disk coordinates $0\le\rho\le1$ the spherical caps with center height $a\in[-1,1]$ have meridian coordinates $$r_a(\rho)=\frac{1+a^2}{2a}\sin(2\rho\arctan a),\qquad z_a(\rho)=\frac{a^2-1}{2a}+\frac{1+a^2}{2a}\cos(2\rho\arctan a),$$ with the removable values $r_0(\rho)=\rho,z_0(\rho)=0$. Rotating these arcs about the vertical axis gives embedded disks joining the lower hemisphere to the upper one and fixing their common circle. The expressions extend smoothly through $a=0$ by their power series; at the axis $r_a(\rho)/\rho$ and $z_a(\rho)$ are smooth functions of $\rho^2$, and at the rim the meridian derivative is nonzero even for $a=\pm1$. Thus these are smooth disk embeddings, not merely a contraction of their images. In a thin rim collar extend their meridian arcs to the stationary annulus outside $D'$, and at the last stage push the resulting disk just past $D$ in its surface-normal collar. This extension is obtained in the normal two-dimensional section by rounding the joining arc and using a cutoff on a slightly larger rim interval; the tangent turns between two nonzero incident directions and the interval is chosen small enough that the curve stays embedded. The sign of the last push is chosen so that the continued outer annulus misses $S$ at the former crossing $C$. Outside that rim collar the last disk is a parallel copy of $D$, disjoint from $S$; compactness supplies one normal width valid on its whole disk. Consequently this is an isotopy of $A$ that replaces its subdisk $D'$ by a disk just past $D$, removes $C$ and every other intersection circle inside $D'$, and creates no new intersections with $S$. Its support is in $B$ and an arbitrarily thin collar of its rim and faces; other annuli are disjoint from that support by step 2.1. Use [F4] to extend it to an ambient isotopy $H$ of $M$, fixed near $\partial M$. Then $H^{-1}(S)$ has fewer intersections with the original $\mathcal A$, since its intersections correspond to those of $S$ with the moved annuli. This contradicts the minimal choice of step 1.1. [A1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

The minimal count must therefore be zero. The ball in the cut piece from step 1.1 is a ball in $M$, and its inverse image under the isotopies bounds the original sphere. This proves irreducibility. If the annulus family is empty, the zero-count argument applies immediately. At no stage was an annulus required to separate, and no boundary-compressibility assertion was used. [F1, step 1.1, step 3.1] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Choose a finite disjoint proper arc system in the base cutting it to disks, avoiding its finitely many exceptional points. Here is a finite construction using [F2]: thicken a finite graph spine by vertex disks and edge bands; a band cocore is an arc with endpoints on the original surface boundary. Cut the bands corresponding to edges outside a spanning tree. The remaining tree of disks and bands is a disk, and the cuts are disjoint. Move the finitely many arc interiors slightly in surface charts to avoid all marked exceptional points. In the resulting disk choose disjoint paths from its exceptional points to one open segment of the original boundary, avoiding the existing cut edges. Construct these successively in the punctured disk; a finite tree joining the points to that segment has a small disk-and-band neighborhood, whose branches may be separated into disjoint paths in the planar cyclic order. The frontier of a narrow neighborhood of each path and its marked point gives a proper arc enclosing just that point. These arcs have endpoints on that original boundary segment and miss the previous cut system. Cutting along them leaves disks with zero or one exceptional point. All arcs remain proper disjoint arcs of the original base and avoid the exceptional points themselves. [F1, F2, given, construct]

Lift these arcs to a finite disjoint family $\mathcal A$ of annuli in $M$. They are proper and two-sided and inject on fundamental groups by [F3]. The components of $M\mathbin{\|}\mathcal A$ retain their Seifert structures over the disks from step 1.1; rounding their boundary corners changes only collars. By [F4] each is a solid torus. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, construct]

A standard solid torus is irreducible. Embed it as one of the standard Heegaard solid tori in $S^3$. A sphere in its interior bounds the two balls of [F6]. The other Heegaard solid torus is connected and disjoint from that sphere, so lies entirely on one of its sides. The opposite closed ball therefore lies in the interior of the original solid torus and bounds the sphere there. Transporting through any supplied solid-torus parameter proves the same assertion for every cut piece of step 2.1. [A1, F6, construct]

The hypotheses of [F5] are now satisfied: the cut pieces are irreducible by step 3.1 and the annuli inject in $M$ by step 2.1. Apply it to conclude that $M$ is irreducible. If no cut was needed, step 3.1 already supplies the conclusion. Thus the nonempty-boundary theorem uses neither a closed Seifert-manifold classification nor a general universal-cover uniformization theorem, and no irreducibility hypothesis has been added to its Statement. [A1, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Projection restricts to a finite orbifold covering $A\to B$: in a regular chart it is a local diffeomorphism, and at a multiplicity-$q$ fiber the transverse chart is $z\mapsto z^q$. The number $n>0$ of intersections with a regular fiber is locally constant and hence constant on the connected regular base. Every base point is reached, since the image is open and closed by these charts and compactness. Since $A$ has boundary, so does $B$. Count lifts of a finite base cellulation with the exceptional points as vertices. Ordinary vertices, edges and faces have $n$ lifts, while a multiplicity-$q_j$ vertex has $n/q_j$. Thus $$0=\chi(A)/n=\chi(B)-\sum_j(1-1/q_j).$$ By [F3], or its graph-spine inequality, $\chi(B)\le1$. If it is zero the sum is zero and there are no exceptional points; $B$ is an annulus or Möbius band. If it is one then $B$ is a disk. Every nonzero summand is at least $1/2$ and less than one, so sum one forces exactly two summands, both $1/2$. These are precisely the three base types of [F5]. Smooth coordinates on the disk, annulus or Möbius base may be used here: the finite graph-neighborhood proof of [F3] can be performed with rounded vertex disks and edge strips. Reversing a free-triangle collapse adds one rounded triangular disk along one interval, preserving the smooth type by [F4]. Rank zero gives a disk; rank one leaves a smooth circle strip whose final interval gluing is increasing or decreasing, giving the standard annulus or Möbius strip by interpolation of interval coordinates. At exceptional points choose the base disk coordinate $w=z^{q_j}$ in one chart; all overlaps away from its center are regular smooth charts. This gives the needed underlying smooth base coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, given, construct]

Cut $M$ along $A$ and cut each fiber at its intersection points with $A$. The segments form an interval bundle: in the regular charts this is the product between two consecutive transverse sheets, and the model $z\mapsto z^q$ has the same segment charts at an exceptional endpoint. Each interval has two endpoints, so the horizontal boundary maps two-to-one onto its segment-space base. The horizontal boundary is exactly the two copies of $A$. If the cut manifold is connected, its interval bundle must be trivial: a nontrivial interval bundle over a connected surface has connected horizontal boundary, whereas here that boundary has two components. Thus in this case the cut manifold is $A\times I$ and $M$ is its mapping torus with return diffeomorphism $g:A\to A$. If the cut is disconnected, there are exactly two pieces, each with horizontal boundary one copy of $A$, and each is the mapping cylinder of a free involution $\tau_i:A\to A$ onto a connected surface $T_i$. Since the total piece is orientable but its interval bundle is nontrivial, $T_i$ is nonorientable. Also $\chi(T_i)=\chi(A)/2=0$ and it has boundary; hence it is a Möbius band by [F3]. In particular both $\tau_i$ reverse orientation. All these descriptions are smooth bundle descriptions: parametrize the segments by a fiber metric length and adjust their end collars to the original transverse charts. No arbitrary annulus self-diffeomorphism is presumed to preserve a circle foliation. [F1, F3, step 1.1, construct]

In the nonseparating case the return map $g$ is a deck map of $A\to B$. Its action is transitive on the $n$ points above a regular point: following its oriented circle fiber passes successively through all intersections before returning. Thus $g^n=1$ on the regular preimage and by continuity on $A$, with no smaller global period. Its finite cyclic group has quotient $B$ with precisely the given exceptional local branch charts. Orientability of the mapping torus forces $g$ to preserve orientation of $A$, so $B$ is orientable. By step 1.1 the possibilities are an annulus without exceptional points and a disk with two order-two points. In the annulus case its connected $n$-fold cover is standard: lift the product base to $\mathbb R\times I$; path lifting identifies the subgroup of its deck group $\mathbb Z$ with $n\mathbb Z$. Thus $A$ has coordinates $(\theta,u)\in S^1\times I$ in which $g$ is a rotation in $\theta$. This is a smooth covering isomorphism, since it is locally the lift of the smooth base coordinates. It preserves the core-circle fibration of $A$. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

In the separating case the two involutions from step 2.1 are also deck maps of $A\to B$. They exchange the endpoints of successive segments of an original fiber. Their group acts transitively on the regular preimage of a base point and is finite: its action on that finite fiber is faithful, since a deck map fixing a point of the connected regular covering fixes it everywhere by unique path lifting, and then fixes all of $A$ by continuity. Since the group contains the orientation-reversing $\tau_i$, the base is nonorientable. Thus step 1.1 makes it the Möbius band with no exceptional points. The covering is unbranched, and its finite deck group is cyclic because $\pi_1(B)=\mathbb Z$. A cyclic group has at most one element of order two; as it is generated by the two involutions, it follows that $\tau_1=\tau_2=\tau$ and the group has order two. The connected double cover of the Möbius band has the standard coordinates $$A=S^1\times[-1,1],\qquad \tau(\theta,u)=(\theta+1/2,-u).$$ This follows by lifting the usual strip model of the Möbius band; its subgroup is $2\mathbb Z$, so the covering isomorphism is smooth and conjugates both involutions simultaneously. The core-circle fibration of $A$ is preserved by both. [F1, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

For the remaining nonseparating base, the orbifold group is $D_\infty=C_2*C_2=\langle a,b\mid a^2=b^2=1\rangle$, as seen by the two puncture loops and their order-two relations in [F2]. Here the covering-subgroup description can be verified directly. The strip $\mathbb R\times[-1,1]$ has the half-turns $a(x,u)=(-x,-u)$ and $b(x,u)=(2-x,-u)$, with disk quotient obtained by folding the vertical sides of $[0,1]\times[-1,1]$. Unfolding this rectangle alternately across those sides gives the entire strip. In any cover, lift one rectangle and extend across successive sides by the local covering charts; the only possible side-return relations are $a^2=b^2=1$, exactly the filled quadratic branch charts. This constructs the covering as the strip modulo its subgroup $H$ of returning lifts, with no general orbifold-cover classification as a premise. A nontranslation half-turn has a fixed point in the strip; membership in $H$ would leave an order-two orbifold point upstairs, which the ordinary annulus does not have. Thus $H$ acts freely, and is a nontrivial translation subgroup: the trivial subgroup would leave the noncompact strip, whereas the given annulus is compact. Write $t=ab$. Reduced words [F6] show that every element is either $t^j$ or $t^j a$, the latter having order two. Hence this subgroup is $\langle t^k\rangle$ for some $k\ge1$. It is normal, and its quotient is the dihedral group of order $2k$. The quotient must also be the cyclic return group of step 3.1. A cyclic quotient would make $t=t^{-1}$ and hence $k\le2$; for $k=2$ the two distinct nonidentity images of $a,b$ give $C_2\times C_2$, not a cyclic group. Therefore $k=1$ and the cover is the double cover. Its explicit model is $$A=S^1\times[-1,1],\qquad g(\theta,u)=(-\theta,-u).$$ Indeed this involution has two fixed points and disk quotient by the two-half-rectangle construction of [F5]. To identify any such cover with this one, delete the two branch points and cut the disk along two arcs from them to its boundary. Over the cut disk the two sheets are separate copies, and gluing across either cut exchanges them, since its local monodromy is the nontrivial order-two permutation. This determines the cover uniquely. The isomorphism extends smoothly over each branch point in its quadratic chart. The base disk identification can agree with the specified linear germs there: [F4]'s interior-germ adjustment is applied in two disjoint point neighborhoods, moving their centers along finite paths avoiding the other point if needed. Thus the cover isomorphism conjugates $g$ to the displayed model. This model again preserves the core-circle fibration. [F1, F2, F4, F5, F6, step 3.1, construct]

In either nonseparating model, fiber $A\times I$ by the core circles at each interval level and descend through its fiber-preserving return map from step 3.1 or 4.1. This is a smooth circle bundle over an annulus or Möbius band, respectively, and its restriction makes the original seam $A$ vertical. In the separating model use the same core circles on the horizontal boundary of each mapping cylinder. They extend through the cylinder and its bottom identification $x\sim\tau x$. The explicit formula of step 3.2 gives the smooth quotient $(A\times[-1,1])/(( \theta,u,v)\sim(\theta+1/2,-u,-v))$, with the common annulus represented at $v=1$. Translation in $\theta$ is a circle action on this quotient. It gives a fibered solid torus with one multiplicity-two core: at $u=0$ the bottom identification is a half-turn of a circle, and away from that core its circle action is free. Thus it has the ordinary local Seifert model of [F1]. On the common annulus the two circle fibrations agree exactly, not merely in slope, so they glue to a smooth Seifert fibration of $M$. It makes $A$ vertical. Finally [F5] and step 1.1 identify the underlying manifold as $T^2\times I$ or $W$. All constructions used actual finite cover and interval-bundle data; an unproved mapping-class theorem for arbitrary annulus diffeomorphisms was not used. [A1, F1, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, step 3.2, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: First suppose the diffeomorphism is the identity on a boundary neighborhood. Conjugate its restriction to the open disk by a fixed smooth diffeomorphism $\operatorname{Int}D^2\to\mathbb R^2$, for example $x\mapsto x/(1-|x|^2)$. Its support becomes compact. A sufficiently large closed square contains that support in its interior; rescale it to $Q=[0,1]^2$. It suffices to construct a smooth isotopy for an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism $f:Q\to Q$ equal to the identity on a neighborhood of $\partial Q$, keeping one common smaller collar fixed. Extend such $f$ by the identity to the plane. No assertion that a round disk is diffeomorphic as a manifold with corners to a square is being used. [given, construct]

Put $Y_0=f_*e_1$, where $e_1=(1,0)$, so $Y_0(z)=Df_{f^{-1}(z)}e_1$. This is a smooth nowhere-zero field equal to $e_1$ on a fixed boundary collar. Write $Y_0=e^a(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ with $a,\theta$ smooth on $Q$ and zero on that collar. For an explicit angle, the one-form $$\omega=\frac{Y_0^1\,dY_0^2-Y_0^2\,dY_0^1}{|Y_0|^2}$$ is closed by differentiation. Its integral on the straight segment from $(0,0)$ to $z$ defines a primitive $\theta$ on the convex square: differentiating the integral and using the equality of its cross partials gives $d\theta=\omega$. The normalized field and $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ then have the same logarithmic derivative and agree at $(0,0)$, so are equal everywhere. Since the boundary collar is connected and $\omega=0$ there, $\theta=0$ there. Take $a=\log|Y_0|$. Define $$Y_t=e^{(1-t)a}\bigl(\cos((1-t)\theta),\sin((1-t)\theta)\bigr).$$ Extend all these fields by $e_1$ outside $Q$. They are jointly smooth and nonvanishing, equal to $e_1$ on one common boundary collar, and join $f_*e_1$ to $e_1$. [step 1.1, construct]

None of the fields $Y_t$ has a periodic orbit. A regular periodic trajectory has a least positive period by its local flow box and uniqueness, and that period parametrizes a simple regular closed curve. Its unit tangent is the field direction. The globally defined angle $(1-t)\theta$, extended by zero off $Q$, would have zero total change on this curve. But [F1] supplies its disk region and [F4] makes the total tangent-angle change $\pm2\pi$, a contradiction. The fields have global flows: they and their first derivatives are bounded since their perturbations of $e_1$ have compact support, so a finite-time orbit cannot escape to infinity and [F2] extends it at every finite endpoint. An orbit starting at $(0,y)$ enters the square and must exit on the right. Indeed an interior orbit cannot meet the invariant horizontal boundary lines by uniqueness, cannot exit left where the field is $e_1$, and, if it never exited, it would stay in the compact square. Then [F3] would give the impossible periodic orbit. The same argument for backward time shows that every point in the square reaches its left edge backwards. At $y=0,1$ the trajectories are just horizontal straight lines. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

Let $\Gamma_t(s,y)$ denote this flow starting at $(0,y)$ at time zero, and let $r(t,y)>0$ be its first time at the right edge. It is smooth in $(t,y)$: near the exit solve $\Gamma_t^1(s,y)=1$ by [F5], whose $s$ derivative is $Y_t^1=1$ there. The analogous backward hitting-time equation gives smooth inverse flow coordinates for every point. Uniqueness prevents distinct starting labels from meeting and prevents a trajectory from meeting itself, by step 3.1. Thus $(s,y)\mapsto\Gamma_t(s,y)$ is a diffeomorphism from the variable strip $0\le s\le r(t,y)$ onto $Q$. Smooth dependence including boundary parameters follows from [F2] and [F5] using the extended fields. Compactness of $(t,y)\in[0,1]^2$ gives finite constants $0<m\le r(t,y)\le M$. The right-edge map $g_t(y)=\Gamma_t^2(r(t,y),y)$ is an increasing smooth interval diffeomorphism, and is the identity near the two endpoints: the field is exactly horizontal on fixed strips near the horizontal edges. [F2, F5, step 3.1, construct]

Choose a smooth function $\rho:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ equal to one near both endpoints, supported in sufficiently short end intervals, with $A=\int_0^1\rho<\min(m,1)/2$. Choose these intervals shorter also than the fixed straight-flow collar width. For $r\in[m,M]$ define $$v_r(x)=\rho(x)+\frac{r-A}{1-A}(1-\rho(x)),\qquad \chi(x,r)=\int_0^x v_r(u)\,du.$$ These functions are smooth, $v_r>0$, $\chi(0,r)=0$, $\chi(1,r)=r$, and $\chi(x,1)=x$. Near the left endpoint $\chi=x$, and near the right endpoint $\chi=r+x-1$, on fixed intervals independent of $r$. Therefore $$E_t(x,y)=\Gamma_t(\chi(x,r(t,y)),y)$$ is a jointly smooth diffeomorphism of $Q$. It equals $(x,y)$ near the left and horizontal edges and equals $(x,g_t(y))$ near the right edge. At $t=0$ uniqueness gives $\Gamma_0(s,y)=f(s,y)$, so $r(0,y)=1$ and $E_0=f$. At $t=1$ the field is $e_1$, so $r(1,y)=1$ and $E_1=\operatorname{id}$. [F2, step 4.1, construct]

Correct the moving right edge. Let $\beta:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ be smooth, equal to one near zero and zero near one. Define $$\Psi_t(x,y)=\bigl(x,\beta(x)y+(1-\beta(x))g_t^{-1}(y)\bigr).$$ Its second-coordinate derivative is positive; its endpoints in $y$ are $0,1$, so it is a diffeomorphism with jointly smooth inverse by [F5]. Near the left edge it is the identity, and near the right it is $(x,g_t^{-1}(y))$. Since $g_t$ is the identity on fixed end neighborhoods, it is also the identity near the horizontal edges. Hence $K_t=\Psi_t\circ E_t$ is the identity on one common collar of every edge. At $t=0,1$ the right-edge map is the identity, so $K_0=f$ and $K_1=\operatorname{id}$. All maps are orientation-preserving, starting so and having everywhere nonzero determinant. This proves the square assertion with joint smoothness, not just continuous dependence of its slices. [F5, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

Extend $K_t$ by the identity outside the square and undo step 1.1's conjugation. A fixed compact subset of the open disk contains all supports, so this is a jointly smooth disk isotopy fixing a common boundary collar. For a diffeomorphism fixing only the boundary pointwise, compare the collar $f\circ c$ with a chosen collar $c$. The explicit collar interpolation and ambient extension in [F1], Proof 5.1, give a smooth isotopy $k_t$ fixing the boundary circle such that $k_1\circ f$ is the identity on a smaller collar. Concatenate $k_t\circ f$ with the just constructed collar-fixed isotopy for $k_1\circ f$. Reparametrize the two time intervals by smooth functions constant near their endpoints and joins. Thus the whole fixed-input smooth isotopy is choice-free. [F1, step 1.1, step 6.1, construct] ∎
