proof_steps.full_text: We induct on $|\mathcal T|+|\mathcal U|$, permitting any connected manifold with the stated boundary and irreducibility properties. If either system is empty, the manifold is itself good; the empty subfamily is consequently a good subfamily of the other system, whose inclusion-minimality forces it to be empty too. This includes the induction base. A minimal system has no product cut component: if a component is $T^2\times I$, one boundary is a cutting face, and absorbing that collar into its neighboring piece preserves that piece up to diffeomorphism and hence preserves goodness. Remove that cutting torus, contradicting minimality. If both ends are the two faces of the same torus, regluing gives a closed connected component of $M$, impossible since $M$ is connected with nonempty boundary. Thus the removal always has a neighboring piece. [A1, F1, given, base, construct]

We record a clean parallel-pair procedure. Every incompressible torus in a supplied product $P=T^2\times I$ is boundary-parallel. Otherwise it is essential; [F5] makes it vertical, since a horizontal torus is impossible over the annulus base. Its projection is an essential circle in that annulus, hence is parallel to a boundary circle, so its inverse image is boundary-parallel after all. An inessential base circle would bound a disk whose inverse image is a solid torus and would compress the torus, excluded by [F1]. The same argument treats a finite torus family simultaneously: verticalize the first, cut along it, and repeat in the product components, keeping their boundary collars fixed. Any already boundary-parallel torus can first be put in its product collar; cutting off that collar leaves products. Finite induction gives an ordered parallel stack. Thus if a torus of one system is parallel, inside a piece of the other system, to a face of that other system, choose the nearest member of the first system in the product stack to obtain a pair bounding a product with no other torus of either system inside. If it were instead parallel to an original boundary of $M$, the nearest member would produce a product cut component of its own system, contradicting step 1.1. The same reasoning excludes parallel pairs within one minimal system. All stack moves use interior smooth isotopies; the closed-surface construction in [F5] has no moving boundary curves and retains a smaller boundary collar at each cut. [F1, F2, F5, step 1.1, construct]

Put the two systems in transverse position by [F2], choosing among such isotopic positions one with least total number of intersection circles. Every intersection circle is essential on both tori. Indeed a circle innermost among the inessential circles on a torus of $\mathcal T$ bounds a disk there whose interior misses $\mathcal U$: any circle inside is inessential on that disk, and a circle essential on its $\mathcal U$ torus would be a compression, contrary to [F1]. Its mate bounds a disk on the $\mathcal U$ torus by incompressibility. Their union, with the rim rounded, bounds a smooth ball. The rest of that $\mathcal U$ torus lies outside the ball, since otherwise the entire torus would lie in the closed ball and [F1] would compress it there; a small ball-collar shrink first places it in the interior if necessary. Every other $\mathcal U$ torus also lies outside, by the same argument and disjointness from the two disk faces. The marked smooth disk sweep of [F3] moves its disk just past the clean disk on $\mathcal T$, deleting this circle and every circle inside the moved disk and creating none. The ball can intersect the reference system $\mathcal T$ during the sweep; its endpoint disk is chosen in a thin collar of the clean face, disjoint from that reference system. This contradicts the least count. Interchanging the systems proves the assertion on both. Consequently the pieces of $\mathcal U$ in a $\mathcal T$ cut piece are annuli and closed tori, and every annulus core has nontrivial image in $M$, hence the annulus is incompressible in that cut piece by [F1]. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

Assume the assertion for every smaller total number of tori. Whenever a clean parallel pair occurs, isotope its member of $\mathcal T$ onto its member of $\mathcal U$ through the product levels and extend by [F2], with support missing all other tori and the original boundary. This isotopy is not required to fix the target torus while moving the first one; the target is the prescribed endpoint position. We then have a common torus. Cut along it. The remaining systems in every connected cut component are still minimal: deleting any nonempty part there while preserving goodness would delete the same part of the original system while retaining the common torus. They are incompressible there, and those components are irreducible by [F1]. Every component has nonempty torus boundary. Each comparison has a strictly smaller total number of tori. Apply the induction hypothesis in each component, fixing smaller collars of the two common faces. Their finite smooth isotopies paste over those fixed collars and extend by the identity to the original manifold. This proves the induction step whenever a clean parallel pair or common torus has been obtained. [F1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, ih, construct]

Every such annulus is boundary-incompressible. Otherwise [F4] makes it boundary-parallel. Its parallelism is a parametrized annulus times an interval, hence a solid torus; its other boundary annulus lies on a single cutting face. Other portions of $\mathcal U$ inside this parallelism are proper annuli whose boundary curves are parallel to its core and have longitudinal coefficient one. There is no whole $\mathcal U$ torus inside it, since [F1] would inject $\mathbb Z^2$ into its cyclic group. In the product boundary coordinates the finitely many parallel curves can be made vertical by finite annulus strip isotopies, retaining the outer rim. Apply [F3]'s primitive-annulus normalization in this solid torus, relative to its boundary. The annulus pieces become disjoint base arcs times the circle; an outermost base arc cuts off an empty disk region against the boundary interval. Its inverse image is an empty annulus parallelism. Pushing that annulus across it and just past the cutting face removes its two boundary intersection circles and creates none. The isotopy extends smoothly by [F2] and is supported away from every other $\mathcal U$ annulus and the original boundary. This contradicts minimality of the count. The annuli are therefore essential. This argument also supplies a clean product when other parallel annuli originally occupied the first parallelism; it does not assume that parallelism was empty. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 2.2, construct]

Suppose an intersection circle $c$ remains on a cutting torus $T$. Its two incident annuli in the other system are essential, so each adjacent piece is Seifert: it either was Seifert or becomes so by [F4]. If the two pieces are different, [F5] permits a choice of fibration on each for which its incident annulus has boundary slope $[c]$. No simultaneous family of annuli is required: this one circle determines the two slopes. By [F6] match and glue these fibrations across $T$. Deleting $T$ preserves goodness, contradicting the minimal system. If both sides belong to the same piece $P$, apply [F5] to the annuli at its two different boundary copies of $T$. Unless $P$ is exceptional, neither application changes its given fibration, so both induced slopes are $[c]$ and [F6] again self-glues to delete $T$. The exceptional $W$ has only one boundary torus, so cannot have two distinct copies of $T$. The exceptional product has exactly two boundary tori, so if those are both copies of $T$, its self-gluing is all of connected $M$ and is closed, contradicting the original nonempty boundary. Thus neither exception occurs in the self-adjacent case. This contradiction proves that the systems are disjoint. [F4, F5, F6, step 1.1, step 3.2, construct]

If a $\mathcal T$ torus lies in an atoroidal $\mathcal U$ piece, it is boundary-parallel there, and step 2.1 supplies a clean parallel pair; step 3.1 completes the proof. The same holds with the systems interchanged. We may therefore assume every torus of either system lies in a Seifert piece of the other, and none is boundary-parallel in that piece. They are essential there. All these Seifert pieces have boundary, so [F5] makes those tori vertical. This can be done simultaneously as follows. First verticalize the $\mathcal T$ tori inside each $\mathcal U$ piece one at a time, cutting along the already vertical tori. Every cut component remains Seifert and irreducible by [F1]. If a remaining torus becomes boundary-parallel, it is parallel to an already cut torus, an original boundary, or a $\mathcal U$ boundary. The first two contradict step 2.1 and minimality; the last supplies a clean parallel pair and finishes by step 3.1. Otherwise [F5] applies again, with supports away from the fixed boundary collars. Then verticalize $\mathcal U$ inside the $\mathcal T$ pieces in the same way, fixing $\mathcal T$ pointwise. Transport the already chosen fibrations of the $\mathcal U$ pieces by these latter isotopies: since $\mathcal T$ is fixed, it remains vertical for them. Retain the fixed fibrations of the $\mathcal T$ pieces while moving their $\mathcal U$ surfaces. Thus each overlap component inherits two actual Seifert fibrations simultaneously, rather than only two separately attainable positions. A $\mathcal U$ piece containing no $\mathcal T$ torus lies entirely in a $\mathcal T$ piece and inherits its restricted fibration, even if its original good label was atoroidal. [F1, F2, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

Fix a torus $U$ of $\mathcal U$, lying in a Seifert $\mathcal T$ piece $P$, and consider the overlap component $C$ incident to one side of $U$ in a $\mathcal U$ piece $Q$. Both its fibrations exist by step 5.1. Its boundary copy of $U$ is injective into $C$: a kernel loop there would be a kernel loop in $M$, contradicting [F1]. If $C$ is neither a product nor $W$, [F6] makes the two fiber slopes equal on $U$. The solid-torus possibility is already excluded by that same boundary injection. If $C=T^2\times I$, its other boundary is a $\mathcal T$ face, a $\mathcal U$ face, or an original boundary. In the first case $C$ is the clean parallelism for step 3.1. In the other two cases there is no $\mathcal T$ boundary of $C$, so it is the whole connected $\mathcal U$ piece $Q$; that is a forbidden product cut component by step 1.1. This includes two distinct faces of one self-adjacent $\mathcal U$ torus. If $C=W$, it has only its one boundary, the indicated face of $U$. Thus again it is the whole $Q$. Replace the fibration of this entire $Q$ by the restriction of the fibration of $P$. There is no other boundary on which this could spoil a match, and no $\mathcal T$ torus inside $Q$. These exhaust the exceptional overlap cases. [F1, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct]

Apply step 6.1 to both sides of $U$. If a clean parallel pair occurs, step 3.1 finishes. Otherwise both adjacent $\mathcal U$ pieces have fiber slope on $U$ equal to that of $P$. In a self-adjacent piece, the two boundary copies are distinct and the nonexceptional slope comparisons use the same fibration; the one-boundary $W$ adjustment cannot be self-adjacent. The two torus fibrations therefore match smoothly by [F6], with their product collars, and their union is Seifert. Delete $U$ from $\mathcal U$. Every other cut piece is unchanged, contradicting its inclusion-minimality. The case where both nonempty systems have no common or clean parallel torus is impossible. Together with the base and common-torus induction this proves the assertion. Every moving surface was carried by a smooth embedding isotopy, and [F2] supplies jointly smooth ambient extensions with supports away from the original boundary. All cut-face comparisons fixed smaller collars, so the finite glued and concatenated isotopies are jointly smooth, stationary at their endpoints, and fixed near $\partial M$. This completes the induction and proves exactly the conditional uniqueness Statement. [F2, F6, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, discharge-induction] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: For an empty family take the identity. Otherwise put the family in general position with the finite strata. First avoid vertices by small supported motions. Transversality to an edge is an open rank condition and gives isolated intersections; compactness away from the avoided endpoints makes their number finite. Use the finite perturbation proof of [F4] near the remaining compact bad set of each edge, keeping the vertex neighborhoods fixed. A surface transverse to an edge is transverse to each incident face there, since the face tangent plane contains the edge tangent. Thus face transversality is already secured near the one-skeleton. For the remaining compact bad sets inside the open faces, the same finite chart-field perturbation proof applies, retaining those fixed neighborhoods. In those charts the face is a closed coordinate plane, so the critical-projection proof applies although the whole open face is not closed in $M$. Finite rank margins preserve earlier transverse conditions. Hence the face intersections form compact one-manifolds with finitely many arc and circle components, and each tetrahedron boundary meets the family in finitely many simple circles with corners at its edges. Write $w=|\mathcal S\cap T^{(1)}|$. [F1, F4, given, construct]

Each individual closed tetrahedron has a smooth embedding parameter from the standard tetrahedron, extending as a local diffeomorphism near every point, using the double of $M$ for charts at its boundary. Indeed its differential on the full-dimensional tangent cone is injective by [F1]; a linear kernel would give two distinct points of that cone with the same image, so the derivative has rank three. The inverse-function and compact separation argument gives an embedding on a neighborhood of that closed tetrahedron. It can consequently be rounded to a supplied smooth ball by rounding a convex standard tetrahedron before applying that parameter. These roundings may be arbitrarily small and avoid the tori near the vertices. Near a torus crossing of an edge, take the edge coordinate $z$ and its two normal coordinates $(x,y)$. Transversality gives the torus as a smooth graph $z=g(x,y)$. Rounding the quadrant in $(x,y)$ rounds the corner of its boundary circle inside that same graph. Along faces ordinary transversality gives the corresponding strip. Thus each original cornered boundary circle has a smooth parallel circle just inside the rounded ball, joined to it by an actual annulus on the torus. The finite graph strips can be chosen disjoint and retain all boundary incidences. This verifies the smooth rim used in the following cap operations rather than treating a cornered sphere as already smooth. [F1, F4, step 1.1, construct]

We spell out the marked ball operations. A proper smooth disk in a parametrized ball splits it into two parametrized balls: cap it with either of the boundary disks supplied by [F3], round the common rim, and apply [F3] in the standard double. The side away from the original ball's exterior is the required inside ball. Restoring the rim gives both disk faces and their collars. Boundary sphere extension in [F3] retains those marked faces, so finitely many disjoint proper disks split a ball into balls, with dual graph a tree. Across a ball bounded by two disk faces there is a smooth disk sweep fixing their common circle. In standard polar disk coordinates it is given by the caps $r_a(\rho)=\frac{1+a^2}{2a}\sin(2\rho\arctan a),\qquad z_a(\rho)=\frac{a^2-1}{2a}+\frac{1+a^2}{2a}\cos(2\rho\arctan a)$ for $-1\le a\le1$, with removable values $r_0(\rho)=\rho$ and $z_0(\rho)=0$. Rotation about the axis gives embedded disks; $r_a(\rho)/\rho$ and $z_a(\rho)$ are smooth in $\rho^2$ at the center, and the meridian derivative is nonzero at the rim. A thin two-dimensional rim collar extends the meridian arcs to the unchanged outer annulus, by graph interpolation between their nonzero incident tangents. Continue the final cap slightly past the target face. Its support lies in the ball and thin rim collars. Applying [F4] realizes this as a jointly smooth ambient disk push. The same meridian arcs with $-1\le\rho\le1$, before rotation, give the smooth arc sweep in a disk bigon; thickening normally gives its strip move. These formulas avoid a nonsmooth conical Alexander interpolation. [A1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct]

An interior surgery disk with boundary on the torus family has nullhomotopic boundary in $M$, hence in that torus by [F2]. A simple nullhomotopic circle on a torus bounds a disk there: lift it to the plane and use [F3]; distinct translates of its bounded disk are disjoint, since two disjoint translated boundary circles could otherwise force proper nesting of bounded equal-area regions. Join this surface disk to the surgery disk and round its rim. Irreducibility gives a smooth ball. No other torus can lie inside, by [F2]. Nor can the punctured remainder of the same torus: it contains a loop essential on the original torus, obtained by moving an essential loop off the removed disk, so lying inside the ball would contradict [F2]. The remainder lies wholly on one side of the sphere, and is therefore on the outside. Thus the marked push of step 3.1 replaces the surface disk by the surgery cap across an empty ball. It is an isotopy of the whole torus family, not a topology-changing compression. All new cap and rim collars may be chosen to miss the one-skeleton whenever the surgery disk does. [F2, F3, F4, step 3.1, given, construct]

In one tetrahedron, process its boundary circles from innermost to outermost on its boundary sphere. Use step 2.1 to put the chosen rim just inside a rounded ball. Choose one common inward collar straightening the torus near those smooth circles: in each transverse graph chart choose an inward vector field tangent to that torus, extend it to the ambient chart, and patch finitely many such fields and ordinary inward fields by finite normalized bumps. Inwardness is convex, and tangency is retained on each disjoint torus; their common-width finite flow therefore makes the torus exactly its boundary circle times the collar interval. Keep all cap depths below this common width. The innermost boundary disk has interior disjoint from the other boundary circles. Push that disk a little inward, keeping its boundary on the torus and choosing the inward rim sector away from that torus; compact separation and its transverse graph collar make this a surgery disk with interior missing the torus family. If the chosen boundary already belongs to a disk component in the tetrahedron, the marked ball parameters from step 3.1 put it in the corresponding thin boundary cap collar. For an enclosing circle put its cap farther inward than the finitely many previously processed caps, still inside that common collar. Its disk interior then misses their terminated vertical strips and caps, while all unprocessed boundary circles outside its boundary disk have disjoint vertical strips. Those caps may be carried along by the same boundary-collar move; their order is retained and no ignored surface is crossed. Otherwise use step 4.1. The annulus from the original rim to its inner smooth rim lies on one side of the replaced disk. If it lies on the retained side, the old circle now bounds that annulus and the new cap; if it lies in the deleted surface disk, the old circle disappears. Either way it leaves the uncapped part, possibly with additional circles deleted as well. Consequently after at most the original number of boundary circles there are only disk components and possible closed components inside the tetrahedron. A closed torus component there is impossible by [F2], and no sphere component was introduced by the disk pushes. Restore the small rounding collars. The resulting intersections with the original tetrahedron are proper disks. The caps and their smaller rim collars lie away from its edges, so $w$ has not increased. [F2, F3, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

Apply step 5.1 to the finitely many tetrahedra in turn. It preserves the disk condition in previously treated tetrahedra: the surgery rim lies inside the current tetrahedron, so in any earlier tetrahedron the deleted surface disk contains whole old disk components or none, and the replacement cap is absent there. Thus it can delete but cannot cut an old disk into a nondisk piece. We obtain disk intersections in all tetrahedra, without increasing $w$. There is then no circle contained in an open face. Such a circle would bound one of these disks on each incident side, making a whole sphere component; on a boundary face it would instead give a whole proper disk component. Both are impossible for the unchanged torus family. [F2, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct]

Suppose a disk in a tetrahedron has boundary crossing some edge more than once. Cut that tetrahedron along the entire disk family. Step 3.1 supplies ball pieces and their dual tree. Traversing the edge records a walk through this tree, with each disk crossing traversing its corresponding edge. Repetition of a disk forces a consecutive inverse pair somewhere: a tree walk with no immediate reversal is its unique reduced path and crosses no tree edge twice. Thus two consecutive surface crossings of the edge belong to the same disk and approach the same cut ball. Join them by a simple arc inside that disk face, and let $\beta$ be the intervening edge segment. Their union is a simple circle on the cut ball's boundary. Its disk side has the parameter of [F3]; after the finite corner rounding of step 2.1, push its interior into the ball, fixing the two edges of its rim. This yields an embedded smooth bigon, with one edge on the torus and the other on the triangulation edge, and with interior missing both the torus family and the tetrahedron boundary. The torus crosses the edge transversely at its two endpoints. This constructs the needed returning-edge bigon from the cut balls, rather than assuming that every long disk boundary has a visible face-return arc. [F2, F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 6.1, construct]

Use the arc sweep of step 3.1 in this bigon, thickened in its normal direction, to move the torus strip past $\beta$. Near each endpoint its transverse graph coordinates continue the moving arc into the unchanged strip; at the last stage the arc lies just beyond $\beta$, and the two edge crossings have disappeared. The meridian-arc derivative stays nonzero during the sweep. Choose the normal thickness below the separation from all other torus sheets and all edges other than $\beta$. Hence no additional edge intersection is created, and $w$ decreases by two. Its ambient extension from [F4] is supported in this neighborhood. Every edge met by an interior torus is an interior edge, since the family and all chosen supports miss a fixed boundary collar. Restore face general position by an arbitrarily small [F4] perturbation fixed near the surviving edge crossings; compact separation from the other edge portions retains the new weight. Redo steps 5.1–6.1, which do not increase $w$, whenever a returning-edge bigon exists. Each full repeat strictly decreases the nonnegative integer $w$, and each disk-making pass is finite. The process therefore terminates. [F4, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1, step 7.1, construct, algebra]

At termination each tetrahedron intersection is a disk crossing every edge at most once. Each face arc consequently joins distinct edges. A simple boundary circle on the tetrahedron's boundary separates its four vertices into two nonempty sets; an edge crosses it exactly when its endpoints are on opposite sides, since it has at most one crossing and each crossing is transverse. A one-versus-three partition gives a triangle boundary and a two-versus-two partition gives a quadrilateral boundary. These are precisely the four triangle and three quadrilateral patterns. Applying step 3.1 to the final disk family gives the stated finite cut-ball parameters, with the restored corner collars. Different quadrilateral partitions cannot occur disjointly, since their two-versus-two partitions are not nested on that sphere. The family has remained smooth at every step by the explicit graph, cap and bigon isotopies and [F4]. Concatenate the finitely many supported ambient isotopies with stationary time changes. They fix the boundary collar and produce exactly the asserted position for the original compatible triangulation. Only the standard smooth ball splitting in [F3] inherited countable choice. No topological-to-PL approximation or arbitrary-marking compatibility was used. [A1, F1, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 6.1, step 8.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: The empty family is independent. Otherwise suppose a relation $\sum_j\lambda_j(i_j)_*[S_j]=0$, with $\lambda_j\in\mathbb F_2$. Choose fundamental cycles $z_j$ on the finitely many $S_j$. By the meaning of homology there is a finite singular three-chain $c$ in $N$ with $\partial c=\sum_j\lambda_j(i_j)_\#z_j$. For $x$ outside the surface union this is a relative cycle in $(N,N\setminus\{x\})$. Write $a(x)\in\mathbb F_2$ for its point-local class in the canonical generator coordinate from [F2]. This function is locally constant on that complement. Indeed a small closed coordinate ball $K$ disjoint from the surfaces contains no point of $\operatorname{supp}\partial c$, so the same chain represents a class in $H_3(N,N\setminus K;\mathbb F_2)$. All its point restrictions over $\operatorname{Int}K$ have the same coordinate by [F1]. Since the complement is connected, $a$ is constant there. The only selections so far are finitely many cycle representatives and a single chain. [F1, F2, given, construct, algebra]

Fix $j$ and a point on $S_j$. Local flatness and separation from the other finitely many compact surfaces give a chart $U=(-2,2)^3$ in which the surface union is exactly $\{x_3=0\}$. Put $K=[-1,1]^3$ and $D=K\cap\{x_3=0\}$. Set $C=N\setminus\operatorname{Int}K$ and $B=C\cup\bigcup_iS_i$. The chain $c$ is a cycle modulo $B$. Its image under [F3]'s connecting map is represented by $\partial c$ modulo $C$. Excision removes the closed set $N\setminus U$, contained in the interior of $C$, for all three relative complexes. Radial retraction $x\mapsto x/\max(1,\lVert x\rVert_\infty)$, with its straight radial homotopy, then identifies the triple with $(K,\partial K\cup D,\partial K)$. It preserves the plane $x_3=0$ and sends the outside of $\operatorname{Int}K$ to $\partial K$. Consequently the local boundary map is $H_3(K,\partial K\cup D)\to H_2(\partial K\cup D,\partial K)$, and the image of $\partial c$ is $\lambda_j[D]$. Here $[D]$ is its relative generator: the compact fundamental cycle of $S_j$ restricts to that generator by [F2], and the other surface cycles are absent from $U$. [F2, F3, step 1.1, construct]

Compute this map in the standard divided cube, not by an unproved global duality assertion. Triangulate its two closed half-cubes compatibly with $D$ and $\partial K$ by [F4]. In the relative degree-three kernel, coefficients of tetrahedra must agree across every interior face outside $D$. The tetrahedra in each half-cube are joined through such faces; for example a generic polygonal path between their interiors crosses faces and avoids the finite codimension-two skeleton. There is no constraint between the halves, since $D$ is omitted in the relative complex. There are no degree-four simplices. Hence the relative group is $\mathbb F_2^2$, with generators the sums of all tetrahedra in the upper and lower half-cube. Each restricts to the nonzero local generator at points in its own open half and to zero in the other; this is the coordinate-ball comparison [F1], after a radial convex-ball parameter for that half-cube. In the relative boundary modulo $\partial K$, either sum has boundary the sum of the triangles of $D$. The target is $\mathbb F_2[D]$, by the same disk-relative finite computation. Thus the connecting map sends $(b_+,b_-)$ to $(b_++b_-)[D]$. The natural relative comparison in [F4] gives exactly this same formula for singular chains. [F1, F3, F4, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Take one point in each open half-cube. The two coordinates $b_+,b_-$ of the localized class of $c$ are respectively its point degrees $a(x_+),a(x_-)$. Steps 2.1–3.1 therefore give $\lambda_j=a(x_+)+a(x_-)$. But both points lie in the connected complement, where step 1.1 made $a$ constant. Their sum is zero. This holds for every $j$, so every coefficient in the original relation vanishes. The argument used only local flat charts, canonical mod-two orientations, finite chains and one finite cube calculation at a time. In particular it permits a one-sided surface, whose two local sides simply belong to the same global complement, and makes no orientability, smoothing, triangulation-existence or choice assertion. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Consider a cut ball $B$ belonging to $C$. Its boundary is divided into horizontal disk copies of $\mathcal S$ and vertical cells from tetrahedron faces. All the latter are rectangles by the hypothesis on $C$. At a segment of a triangulation edge exactly two such rectangle sides meet in this ball, since a tetrahedron has two faces there. No vertex of the tetrahedron belongs to $B$: every face region incident to such a vertex is a nonrectangular corner region. Thus the union $V$ of the vertical rectangles is an interval bundle over a finite one-manifold, obtained by gluing the base intervals of rectangles at their endpoints. The glued vertical edges are its interval fibers. Every base vertex has degree two, so each connected base component is a circle. Its total space is an annulus or a Möbius band according as the interval return map preserves or reverses endpoints. This follows directly by cutting that circle once; an increasing return homeomorphism is interpolated to the identity by $(1-s)g(t)+st$, while a decreasing one is interpolated to the reflection. The Möbius case cannot be a subsurface of the oriented boundary sphere of $B$. Hence every component of $V$ is an annulus, with its interval fibers. [F1, given, construct]

Each boundary circle of $V$ is the whole boundary circle of one horizontal disk. A horizontal disk has only one boundary, so it meets exactly one annulus end. The boundary sphere of $B$ is connected; the incidence graph of these disks and annuli consequently consists of two disks and a single connecting annulus. Choose product coordinates on that annulus retaining its given interval fibers: trivialize around its base circle by the increasing-return interpolation in step 1.1. Parametrize each horizontal disk with the induced boundary coordinate, extending its circle reparametrization radially by [F2]. These maps give a boundary homeomorphism from the boundary of $D^2\times I$ to $\partial B$, taking horizontal disks and every vertical fiber to the specified ones. A radial extension over a standard convex ball, followed by the supplied parameter of $B$, extends that boundary map to a homeomorphism $D^2\times I\to B$. Thus every rectangular-only cut ball has a product parameter. No uniqueness of ball parameters or smooth Alexander interpolation is claimed or needed. [F2, step 1.1, construct]

Choose each physical face rectangle's fiber arcs once, using its supplied parameter, and use those same arcs on the two incident balls in step 2.1. Their product parameters then identify the shared rectangle by a fiber-preserving map. Near the interior of its base edge, write that map as $(s,t)\mapsto(f(s),g(s,t))$. The base map $f$ is a homeomorphism and every $g(s,-)$ is an interval homeomorphism; extending these same maps constantly in the collar-normal coordinate gives an interval-bundle chart over the glued base strip. At a base vertex, the balls are those incident to one segment of the original one-skeleton. Their normal sectors have a cyclic link by [F1]; their interval identifications around that cycle compose to the identity, since they identify the same actual points of that segment. To see extension at that center explicitly, cut the polygonal vertex star along one radial line and trivialize its finitely many product sectors in order. At a small base radius the return interval map is increasing, depends continuously on the radius and tends to the identity at radius zero, since its edge maps telescope there. Interpolate its inverse to the identity by convex combinations of increasing interval maps while unwinding the angular coordinate across the cut. This cancels the return map. The correction tends uniformly to the identity at the center, so it extends continuously to the central interval and gives a disk times an interval there. The base is the finite complex formed by gluing the disk bases of the balls along the indicated edge intervals. Its face interiors, edge interiors and vertex stars are respectively disks, strips and disks. It is consequently a compact connected surface without boundary, and these constructions give an interval bundle with total space $C$. [F1, step 1.1, step 2.1, construct]

This component cannot meet the original boundary. A boundary triangle has no intersections with the closed interior torus family; its whole face is a nonrectangular region. A component reaching a boundary edge or vertex likewise reaches such a region by its half-space local charts. Thus every boundary component of $C$ is one of its cutting torus faces. The base also has an explicit finite surface cellulation: use the disk bases and paired edge intervals just constructed, reparametrize their finitely many boundary edges once, and extend each boundary reparametrization radially over its disk. The edge gluings can then be made linear. For an explicit regular subdivision, insert disjoint small vertex disks, edge rectangles and the remaining polygon interiors in its finite surface stars. Triangulate these finitely many pieces with matching boundary subdivisions by [F2]. This separates repeated incidences and gives a finite surface triangulation. In particular the base has a compact metric and a finite interval-bundle trivializing cover. [F1, F2, step 3.1, construct]

To produce an actual core without assuming all interval transitions are already affine, take such a finite trivializing cover $U_i$ of the base. It has continuous nonnegative weights summing to one: in its finite-complex metric use $d(q,Q\setminus U_i)$, taking the constant one when $U_i=Q$, and normalize their finite positive sum. Here $Q$ temporarily denotes the abstract base. In the fiber over $q$, give the $i$th interval chart normalized Lebesgue measure and combine these measures with those weights. Terms outside $U_i$ are zero. This defines an intrinsic atomless probability measure of full support on each fiber. In any chosen local orientation of the fiber, its cumulative distribution is jointly continuous in the base and interval coordinate, strictly increasing from zero to one. Joint continuity follows from the finite sum of the continuous coordinate changes on the charts; at a chart's boundary its bounded contribution tends to zero with its weight. Hence its unique midpoint varies continuously: two strictly bracketing distribution values continue to bracket under a small change of the base point. The midpoint is a section. Its signed cumulative coordinate identifies every fiber with $[-1,1]$, and on overlaps the new coordinates differ only by $u\mapsto u$ or $u\mapsto-u$, depending on which endpoint was chosen as initial. This reduces the bundle to an ordinary linear interval bundle. [step 3.1, step 4.1, construct]

The image of that section is now a compact connected locally flat embedded core, again denoted $Q$: in each bundle chart it is the plane $u=0$ in a disk times an interval. The two local sides form the endpoint-orientation double cover of the base. If that cover is disconnected, either of its two components supplies a global endpoint choice, and the cumulative coordinate trivializes $C$ as $Q\times I$. Its two boundary components are tori by step 4.1, so $Q$ is a torus and $C$ is $T^2\times I$. If $C$ is not that product, the endpoint cover is connected, the core has no global choice of side, and it is one-sided. Removing the core gives a bundle of half-open intervals over that connected double cover; local products and connected fibers make its total space connected. Equivalently, radial contraction of each half-fiber onto its endpoint is a deformation retraction onto that cover. All choices of rectangles, parameters, charts and weights were finite, and the midpoint was unique. This proves the asserted interface and its topological category. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, construct] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: Apply [F1]; its ambient diffeomorphism preserves the no-product condition. In a triangular face the normal arcs have three types, according to the pair of distinct edges they join. Arcs of one type occur in a parallel stack about their common vertex: otherwise two of them separate each other's endpoints and would intersect in the disk. Between consecutive arcs of a stack is a rectangle, with two opposite surface edges and two original edge segments. Collapse each such strip for this count. There remains at most one arc of each type, so at most three disjoint arcs and hence at most four regions. All nonrectangular regions survive as distinct regions of this collapsed picture. Thus there are at most four nonrectangular regions per face, and at most $4t$ overall. The face cells have actual disk parameters: cut the parametrized triangular disk successively along its finitely many disjoint smooth proper arcs. At each cut the arc and either boundary side form a Jordan circle with finitely many corners; [F4]'s finite rounding and restoration give its two disk parameters retaining those corner arcs. Induction gives every face-cell parameter. A rectangle's four boundary intervals then specify its product boundary map, extended over that disk by [F4]. All input rectangle and cut-ball parameters for [F2] are therefore supplied. [A1, F1, F4, given, construct]

Write $n=|\mathcal S|$, and let $v$ be the number of cut components. Let $m$ be the number of components meeting faces only in rectangles. By [F2] and the no-product hypothesis they have disjoint one-sided compact locally flat cores $Q_1,\ldots,Q_m$, and removing a core keeps its component connected. Every other component contains a nonrectangular face region. A physical face region belongs to only one cut component: its two incident tetrahedral regions are glued across its interior, or it is an original boundary face with one incident side. Thus distinct components can be assigned distinct nonrectangular regions, using a fixed order on their finite set. Consequently $v\le m+4t$. [F2, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Form the finite connected dual graph of the torus cuts, with one vertex for each cut component and one edge for each torus, including loops. Choose a spanning tree and let the other $k$ edges correspond to $S_1,\ldots,S_k$. Gluing all the tree edges keeps the union connected, so cutting only these $k$ tori leaves a connected manifold. In the fully cut manifold remove all the cores $Q_j$. Each piece remains connected by [F2]. Regluing the same tree edges again gives a connected space. In the uncut manifold this says exactly that the complement of $S_1\cup\cdots\cup S_k\cup Q_1\cup\cdots\cup Q_m$ is connected; the small cut-face collars merely supply the adjacent open product neighborhoods. All these surfaces are compact, closed, disjoint and locally flat. The tree has $v-1$ edges, so $k=n-v+1$, equivalently $v=n-k+1$. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Pass to $N=\operatorname{Int}M$ to apply [F3]. The finite boundary collar in [F5] can be chosen disjoint from the displayed compact surfaces. In its coordinate $r\ge0$, choose a nonnegative cutoff $\chi$, equal to one near zero and zero beyond a smaller collar, and a sufficiently small $\epsilon>0$. The map $r\mapsto r+\epsilon\chi(r)$ pushes $M$ into its interior and fixes all the surfaces. The homotopy $r\mapsto r+s\epsilon\chi(r)$ proves that the interior inclusion is a homotopy equivalence, since the same homotopy starting at a positive $r$ stays in the interior. It also proves that their complement in $N$ is connected: its pushed image is connected by step 3.1, and every interior point is joined inside that complement to its pushed image. By [F3], the $k+m$ surface classes are independent in $H_2(N;\mathbb F_2)$, and therefore in $H_2(M;\mathbb F_2)$ under this homotopy equivalence. Hence $k+m\le\beta$. No simultaneous triangulation of the possibly one-sided cores has been assumed; their independence is the local singular-chain jump theorem [F3]. [F3, F5, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

Combine $n-k+1=v\le m+4t$ with $k+m\le\beta$ to obtain $n+1\le k+m+4t\le\beta+4t$, as claimed. This applies also to the empty family; its one cut component contains a nonrectangular face region. The bound uses the original fixed compatible triangulation, so it is uniform over every finite stage of a process satisfying the hypothesis. Such a process cannot make more cuts than this fixed integer. Countable choice was inherited only in [F1]'s smooth ball splitting; every other selection was finite, and the homology computation used finite matrices and the choice-free local jump argument. In particular no full AC, arbitrary-marking triangulation bridge or PL-to-smooth irreducibility assertion entered. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: The exterior is a compact oriented smooth manifold with torus boundary. To verify the last assertion, orthonormalize the global normal frame of [F2] in the metric used for the tube's disk subbundle. Its chosen tube is then smoothly parametrized by $S^1\times D^2$, so its boundary is $T^2$. The exterior is connected as well: any two distinct points in it are joined by an embedded great-circle arc in $S^3$ (choose a half great circle in the antipodal case). Apply [F6]'s compact relative transversality to this arc and the knot, fixing its endpoint neighborhoods. A transverse one-dimensional arc cannot meet the one-dimensional knot in a three-manifold, so it avoids the knot. There is a continuous retraction $S^3\setminus K\to E_K$, equal to the identity outside the tube and sending a nonzero normal vector of length $r\le\epsilon$ radially to the vector of length $\epsilon$ in the same direction. It is continuous at the tube boundary and fixes both endpoints. The retracted arc is a path in the exterior. The coincident-endpoint case is constant. Thus $E_K$ is connected, and it is irreducible by [F1]–[F2]. [F1, F2, F6, given, construct]

Choose the finite compatible triangulation of [F3] once. If $E_K$ itself is atoroidal or Seifert, the empty family proves existence and is minimal. Otherwise start with the empty family, and whenever a current component $C$ is neither atoroidal nor Seifert, choose an incompressible torus not boundary-parallel in $C$, by [F8]'s definition of failure of atoroidality. It is two-sided: the torus and ambient orientations orient its normal line, and a finite normal-field flow gives a smooth product neighborhood. Every cut component has nonempty torus boundary. Indeed a boundaryless cut component would have no cutting face and no original boundary, hence would give a closed component of the original connected exterior, impossible by step 1.1. Irreducibility of the successive pieces will follow from [F5]. This construction is needed only for a bounded finite number of steps, as established below. [F3, F5, F8, step 1.1, construct]

Suppose a finite accumulated family is incompressible in $E_K$. By [F5] its cut pieces inject into $E_K$ and are irreducible. A new torus chosen in $C$ injects into $C$ by [F6], and then into $E_K$ by composition. It is therefore incompressible in $E_K$ by [F6]. The empty family starts this induction. Thus every finite stage consists of incompressible tori in the original exterior and has irreducible cut pieces, and all applications of [F4]–[F5] are within their smooth categories. [F5, F6, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

No finite stage has a product cut component. Initially the exterior is not good, hence is not $T^2\times I$. If a product first appears after a new cut along $T\subset C$, it must be one of the new components and must contain a boundary copy of $T$. If its other end is an old boundary face of $C$, the displayed product makes $T$ boundary-parallel in $C$, contradicting its choice. If both ends are the two copies of $T$, regluing them makes the entire connected old component $C$ a closed torus bundle; this contradicts the nonempty boundary of $C$ verified in step 2.1. Components unaffected by this cut were already nonproducts. This finite induction proves the no-product condition required by [F4], without assuming that selected tori separate. [F4, F8, step 2.1, step 3.1, construct]

Put $B=4t+\beta-1$, a fixed finite integer from [F4]. If no stage had become good after at most $B$ cuts, the construction could be extended through $B+1$ cuts by finite induction: at each of these finitely many stages use step 2.1. Steps 3.1 and 4.1 would then give an incompressible torus family with no product cut component and $B+1$ members, contradicting [F4]. Thus a finite good family exists. This argument selects only a bounded finite list of cuts, rather than postulating an infinite sequence of independent choices. The zero-cut empty family in the nongood initial case also satisfies [F4], so $B\ge0$ there. [F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, construct, algebra]

Among the subfamilies of that particular finite good family, take a good subfamily of least cardinality. There is at least one, and its finite power set suffices for the selection. No proper subfamily can be good, so it is inclusion-minimal in exactly [F8]'s sense. This proves existence with all the original hypotheses and no additional condition on the knot. [F8, step 5.1, construct, choose]

Finally let two finite inclusion-minimal systems as in the Statement be given. Step 1.1 verifies that their ambient exterior is compact, connected, orientable and irreducible with nonempty torus boundary. Their tori and good cut pieces have exactly [F7]'s smooth hypotheses. Apply that full uniqueness supplier to obtain a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $E_K$, even fixed near its boundary, carrying one system to the other. The underlying convention is the ordinary smooth ambient isotopy of the knot definitions; no homeomorphism isotopy has replaced it. The conclusion asserts only atoroidal or Seifert pieces and introduces no hyperbolicity assertion. [F1, F7, F8, step 1.1, step 6.1] ∎

proof_steps.full_text: By [F1] refine so $T$ is a full subcomplex. At a vertex of this subcomplex its surface link is a PL circle embedded in the standard PL two-sphere which is the ambient interior vertex link. The latter has a supplied standard parameter from the PL manifold triangulation. By [F2] the circle bounds two PL disks. Parametrize both by standard polygonal disks. Their boundary parameters can be matched: a PL circle homeomorphism extends by coning a common finite subdivision of its domain and target circles to their disk centers. The two disk maps then give a PL homeomorphism of the link pair to a standard sphere with its equatorial polygonal circle. Coning this pair map to the ambient vertex gives a PL chart in which $T$ is a flat plane. The finitely many open vertex stars cover $T$, and each chart flattens the whole surface portion in its star. Thus local PL flatness has been established from the link disks, not inferred from the given merely topological product map. [F1, F2, given, construct]

Cut the finite ambient complex along the full surface subcomplex: keep the original three-simplices, cease gluing across its two-faces and distinguish incident vertex and edge copies according to their local sides. The finite flat charts of step 1.1 show that each local side is a PL half-space. The result is a compact finite PL three-manifold; its new boundary projects to $T$ as the finite PL two-sheeted side cover. The given topological product neighborhood labels these sides continuously by the sign of its interval coordinate. This trivializes that cover: its two labeled parts project bijectively and locally piecewise linearly to $T$, hence are PL copies $T_+$ and $T_-$. No assertion that the original product map was PL has been made. Face subdivisions distinguish any repeated quotient incidences and give a finite compatible triangulation of this cut space. [F1, step 1.1, construct]

Apply [F3] to its two new boundary copies. Shrink the compact collars so they miss each other and the old ball boundary; finite compact separation gives one width. Reglue $T_+$ to $T_-$ by their pointwise identical projection to $T$. Their two PL collars then give a PL bicollar $T\times[-\epsilon,\epsilon]\to B$. Its finite product triangulation can be fitted to the ambient finite triangulation by [F1]. Thus all the local-flatness, finite-triangulation and product-collar inputs of [F4] are now supplied, including when the initial two-sided neighborhood was only topological. [F1, F3, step 2.1, construct]

If there were no PL compressing disk, [F4] would inject $\pi_1(T)=\mathbb Z^2$ into $\pi_1(B)=1$, impossible by [F5] and radial contraction in the supplied ball parameter. Therefore [F4] gives an embedded PL disk meeting $T$ exactly in its boundary, which does not bound a PL disk on $T$. By [F2]'s surface disk criterion this boundary is nontrivial in $\pi_1(T)$, hence essential. Its interior may be taken on one of the cut sides: the constructive implication in [F4], Proof 1.2 and 4.1, applies finite PL Loop to a noninjective cut face and gives a disk proper in that cut component. In particular it avoids the old boundary of $B$. Alternatively any contact with that old boundary can be removed by the PL boundary collar in [F3]: choose its width disjoint from $T$ and map its height $r$ to $\delta+(1-\delta/(2\eta))r$ for $0\le r\le2\eta$, keeping heights beyond $2\eta$ fixed, with $0<\delta<2\eta$. This gives a path in $E$. Construct a two-sided collar of $T$ by choosing its outward normal field, extending it in finitely many slice charts by normalized finite bumps, and applying the compact-flow construction of [F3]. Its local inverse and compact separation estimates give a common positive width. Take $U$ to be $N$ with a short exterior collar adjoined, and $V$ to be $E$ with a short interior collar adjoined. They are open, cover $S^3$, and intersect in the full torus collar. Collapsing the respective added collar coordinates gives retractions to $N,E,T$, with the original inclusions as the resulting homology maps. This does not change or enlarge the supplied tube. Give the core circle its one-vertex one-edge CW structure and the boundary torus its square quotient structure, with one vertex, two factor edges and a two-cell attached by their commutator. The endpoint incidences and the commutator exponent sums are zero, so [F1] gives $H_1(N;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ and $H_1(T;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z[\mu]\oplus\mathbb Z[\sigma]$, where $\mu$ is the fiber meridian and $\sigma$ is the core section. Projection $p$ sends $\mu$ to zero and $\sigma$ to one. The segment of [F1]'s sequence for step 1.1 is $0\to H_1(T)\to H_1(N)\oplus H_1(E)\to0$, with middle map $(p_*,-i_*)$. It is therefore an isomorphism. Restricting it to $\ker p_*=\mathbb Z[\mu]$ identifies that subgroup with $0\oplus H_1(E)$: for any $(0,y)$ its unique preimage must have projection zero. Thus $H_1(E)$ is infinite cyclic generated by $i_*[\mu]$. Write $i_*[\sigma]=k\,i_*[\mu]$. Its kernel on the torus is exactly $\mathbb Z([\sigma]-k[\mu])$, whose generator has core projection one. Only the finite circle and torus complexes were used; no disk CW structure, universal coefficients or Alexander duality is required. [F1, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

Let $c$ be the essential boundary of the given disk. It is primitive by [F2] and has zero homology image in $E$. Step 2.1 makes its class an integral multiple of $[\sigma]-k[\mu]$, and primitivity forces that multiple to be $\pm1$. Orient it with core projection $+1$, so its class has coordinates $(1,a)$ in core-then-meridian order. By [F2] it admits a smooth torus isotopy to $\gamma_a(s)=(e^{2\pi is},e^{2\pi ias})$. Choose its circle parametrization so the final parametrization is this one: precompose by the inverse final circle map. Denote the resulting smooth isotopy by $c_t(s)=(u_t(s),z_t(s))$, with $|z_t|=1$. Choose a smooth $\tau(r)$ equal to zero near $r=1$ and one near $r=1/2$. For $1/2\le r\le1$ use $e(u_{\tau(r)}(s),r z_{\tau(r)}(s))$; for $0\le r\le1/2$ use $e(e^{2\pi is},r e^{2\pi ias})$. The two formulas agree on an open seam collar. Distinct positive radii separate their images, and each radius has an embedded circle. At zero the two derivatives are the core tangent and the nonzero meridian-plane vector, hence independent. This is a smooth embedded annulus from the exact curve $c$ to the core $K$, otherwise inside $N$. [F2, step 2.1, construct, algebra]

Join that annulus to the exterior disk. They meet only along $c$. Smooth the rim while fixing the core boundary. Here the local smoothing is explicit: frame the normal plane of $c$ by its transverse direction in the oriented torus and the torus normal. Compactness and [F3]'s finite flows give a common product coordinate $(s,y,q)$, with $T$ given by $q=0$. The exterior disk and tube annulus are graphs $y=h_\pm(s,q)$ on the two signs of $q$, by their transverse inward directions. Their common value at zero agrees. Convolve across $q=0$ with a small smooth compactly supported kernel and cut off the correction before the rim collar ends. This gives a smooth graph, fixed outside the collar; projection to $(s,q)$ retains embedding. The construction is periodic in $s$ and has one compact width. Reparametrize the original disk's boundary collar to the annular collar by [F2]; attaching an annulus to a disk then gives the usual parametrized disk by radial rescaling of that source collar. We have obtained a smooth embedding $f:D^2\to S^3$ with boundary exactly $K$. [F2, F3, step 3.1, construct]

Such a supplied disk parameter gives an actual smooth unknotting. Its circles $f(r s)$, $s\in S^1$, shrink smoothly from $r=1$ to a fixed small positive radius; the circle never collapses to a point. Choose a point off this compact disk and the fixed standard spanning disk. Each is closed with empty interior by its finite smooth graph charts, and a finite union of closed sets with empty interior still has empty interior, so such a point exists without choice. Its positive stereographic chart contains both disks. At the first disk center write its chart map as $p+F(x)$ with $F(0)=0$. For sufficiently small fixed $\eta>0$, the circles $p+F(t\eta s)/t$, continued at $t=0$ by $p+\eta\,dF_0(s)$, form a smooth embedded-circle isotopy. The Taylor integral formula gives the smooth continuation; derivatives on a small disk are uniformly close to the injective linear derivative, and projection onto its two-dimensional image plus integration on segments proves injectivity. Gram-Schmidt writes that derivative as an orthonormal two-frame times an upper-triangular matrix with positive diagonal. Interpolating that matrix to the identity keeps the diagonal positive, so turns the ellipse into a round circle through embeddings. Repeat this at the fixed standard disk. Join the resulting round circles by translation of their centers, positive-radius interpolation and a path of rotations of their positive three-frames; successive coordinate-axis rotations give such a finite smooth path. Reverse the second disk's isotopies. A half-turn about a diameter corrects the circle orientation if required and still preserves ambient orientation. Thus the original oriented $K$ is joined to the fixed standard oriented unknot through smooth embedded circles in one compact track. Apply [F3], with stationary time changes at all joins, to obtain a jointly smooth ambient isotopy starting at the identity. All its diffeomorphisms preserve orientation.
